title: Hungry Thirsty Roots: Imagining and Constructing Ethnic Otherness in 1800s England
abstract: My research is a historical ethnography of depictions of the ethnic and cultural other in 19th century England. I was motivated to do this research by curiosity about how cultural and racial otherness and national belonging was constructed historically. Although my work does not directly relate to modern conceptions of national belonging, I was inspired to do my research by seeing ideas about this shift during my own lifetime. My work is a historical ethnography of depictions of immigrants to England in the 1800s in various mediums. Some of the materials I used are presented as fictional by their authors, like Dracula and Goblin Market, while others are presented as nonfiction, like the political cartoons of George Cruikshank. From these materials I draw two primary conclusions. The first is that perceived racial difference is not based fully on physical differences and instead is heavily influenced by cultural factors. The second is that “foreignness” or racial difference is thought of as having a supernatural quality that presents a social, sexual, and political threat. Not being “of the nation” is construed as being inhuman, magical and sinister. My work adds the anthropological understanding of national belonging and racial identification that’s already been studied in ethnographies like Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power by Laura Ann Stoler and has implications regarding modern modes of thought about immigrants, race, and citizenship.

title: "His Name Is Lancelot" Spamalot Choreography
abstract: Winter quarter at Northwestern can be a difficult time for students as the harsh weather and rigorous classwork can feel like a heavy weight to bear. For this reason, we were extremely excited to choreography Monty Python’s Spamalot, a musical produced in Winter 2020 by the Northwestern student theatre production board Lovers & Madmen. The production was presented to us as a source of joy and laughter for the students who came to see it during winter quarter. Spamalot, adapted from the film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, spoofs both Arthurian legend and the tropes of the musical theatre canon. In the middle of act two, the number “His Name Is Lancelot” presents King Arthur’s bravest knight, Sir Lancelot, discovering and eventually embracing his sexuality through a disco-infused musical sequence. The number is a celebration of self-acceptance and LGBTQI+ pride, and we highlighted the joy presented in this number through the choreography. By using popular LGBTQI+ dance forms, including waacking and voguing, we created a piece that celebrated LGBTQI+ culture instead of portraying stereotypes that are often presented in the choreography of this number. We fostered an environment of play and creativity while teaching this number so that our dancers could feel supported and proud of the work they were putting into the piece. We challenged our dancers to push themselves out of their comfort zones while still playing to their strengths so that we were able to both teach them new forms of dance while letting them shine with their own individuality and sense of self-acceptance. We are proud to say that the joy and laughter created from this piece helped to lift some of the winter quarter weight from the dancers who performed and the audience members who observed. The performers seen in this video are Nathan Karnik as Lancelot, Clay Lawhead as Prince Herbert, and Jay Towns, Rick Hilscher, Zeke Albro, Alexander Christie, and Jude Cramer as the Dance Ensemble.

title: - Northwestern's Office of Undergraduate Research -
abstract:
“Research has allowed me to apply what I learn about in classes to something that feels much more tangible and applicable to the real-world. Challenging yourself to think outside of the "lecture" box is something I've found to be extremely important and fulfilling.” - 2019 Summer URG Student
The Office of Undergraduate Research awards funding to hundreds of students each year; a majority of these students are engaged in independent research and creative projects where they learn project management skills that will support their post-college aspirations.  Students learn how to explore a topic of significant interest in-depth: first, they learn to collect and interpret scholarly literature to frame a rationale around their research question, supported by expertise from faculty experts (inside and outside the university) to determine what gaps in their field of study need to be filled.  Next, they learn how to develop a project and methodology that could potentially fill that gap, wrestling with the real world limitations of time and their current skill level.  They learn how to write a competitive grant proposal (ultimately reviewed by multiple faculty across a range of disciplines) with iterative revisions based on feedback from faculty sponsors and OUR advisors.  Once awarded, students learn that life rarely goes according to plan, even if the plan is meticulously constructed with expert advice.  Consequently, they adjust and revise their projects, learning to be creative and determined, and show grit and imaginative resourcefulness.  Finally, they learn to analyze and draw conclusions from their results and relevant findings. Many students render what they learned into papers and presentations to share their new knowledge with the broader world, whatever that may be. 
We hope that in the process they discover magnificent things, but we know that the true value is in the experience itself.  Confident in the process of knowledge acquisition, curated by thinking in terms of questions and how to answer them (instead of existing answers), students are now more prepared for the life ahead of them, whether that be graduate school, industry, non-profit work, creative artistry, or entrepreneurship.  It is this process that makes undergraduate research such a high impact practice, and it is our emphasis on helping students to gain this experience that makes Northwestern an innovative and leading voice in this field.
OUR is an advising-centric office.  We assume you don’t know how to develop your own project or find a lab, and that is why we are here for you.  Set up an individual advising appointment now: https://undergradresearch.northwestern.edu/advising-request

title: A Cat Called Kush: Studies on Harmony and Dialogue Across Media
abstract:
In the fall of 2018, I participated in Northwestern University’s semester-long Art, Literature, and Contemporary European Thought program in Paris, France, in association with two French universities: Sciences Po and Université Sorbonne Nouvelle III. During the program, I was able to conduct research on some of the most significant art works and literary achievements of the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries. This program inspired a project I completed during the summer of 2019, when I was awarded a Northwestern Summer Undergraduate Research Grant for a practice-based study that explored how the same stories can be told through different media. Over the course of nine weeks, I completed a series of interrelated art works, all relating to the experiences I had while studying in France. I began with notes, sketches, and painted studies of photographs I had taken of the city. From these sketches, I began my first large scale oil painting. During this time, I started writing a short fiction story, a narrative inspired by the notes and the overall process of my first painting. I continued experimenting with this method of production, completing three large oil paintings, a graphite drawing, a book of sketches, a series of short fiction stories, and a sculptural piece by the end of the summer. My project concluded in September 2019, when the pieces were installed in Northwestern’s Kresge Centennial Hall gallery space. The exhibition demonstrated my efforts to harmonize color, image, and the written word. 

My own creative process as a writer and artist is inspired by the coalescence of painting, illustration, and literature. One of the works of art that has motivated my own practice is "Prose on the Trans-Siberian Railway and of Little Jehanne of France" (1913) by Sonia Delaunay. This piece unites both color and text through abstract painting and free verse poetry, and is presented on a tall, vertically orientated sheet of creased parchment with two distinct halves. On the left side, Delaunay’s colorful circles, blotches, and swirls subtly bleed into the right-hand column, which features a poem written by the novelist and poet Blaise Cendrars. While the painting explores how colors interact with one another and the poem tells the story of a voyage by train, both are presented by the artist and the writer as one. Both share themes of movement, a journey shown through story and color. For me, this piece raises an important question: what new form is created when existing media are combined? Similarly, the surrealist novel "Nadja," by André Breton, has inspired my own artistic studies. His striking use of photographs, sketches, and portraiture within the textual narrative of the story seem to blur the boundaries between reality and fiction, something that I am exploring in my creative work today. I am drawn to the locations where media intersect, and the interdisciplinary forms that are produced within that space.

title: A Modest Moral Realism
abstract: This project emerged from my desire to explore the nature of moral truth as it compares to other sorts of truth, which is a critical topic in moral philosophy. If we accept science as eminently “real,” how “real” is morality? I approached this question by diving into foundational scholarship in the philosophy of science and meta-ethics, particularly from Kant, Hume, Richard Boyd, Arthur Fine, Bernard Williams, and Hilary Putnam. Through my reading, I came to view scientific reality as a matter of humanity’s observation. That which is “scientifically real” is that which we happen to receive through our physical senses. We cannot claim any deeper ontology for physical reality than that we all experience it. Accordingly, it seemed to me that morality would maintain a similar level of reality to physicality if it achieved a similar experiential consensus. On analysis, it appeared that such experiential consensus is roughly met by morality, with some important caveats. I then composed a paper arguing for each of these findings. By taking science and morality from the heavens and placing them on the ground, my paper defends moral truth as an empirical discovery, just like scientific truth. The significance of my paper is its commentary on how we ought to view moral thought. I argue that if scientific advancement represents progress towards truth, moral development does as well. If I am right, morality deserves a seat directly next to science at the table of empirical human knowledge.

title: A Scalable Quantum Network Architecture
abstract: Quantum communication enables the cryptographically secure transfer of information. A highly anticipated application is the construction of a large-scale quantum internet, which in principle could utilize optical cables from the existing classical internet as communication channels. The classical internet exhibits a complex topological structure with the presence of highly connected hubs; however, current proposals for the construction of quantum networks are either difficult to scale up to a large number of nodes, or lead to a non-complex network structure. Is it possible to design quantum networks with a complex topology for thousands of nodes or more? Here, we use computational simulations to create scalable complex quantum networks by strategically linking magnetic domains in disordered compounds. Using the two-dimensional quantum Ising model, a mathematical model of the magnetic behavior of solid layers, we computationally generate the quantum networks obtained when magnetic domains in one layer are linked to one another using magnetic domains in another layer. We then analyze these networks to determine if they exhibit complex network topologies with highly connected hubs present. Preliminary results suggest that it is indeed possible to create complex network topologies with thousands of nodes, a proof of concept which motivates further theoretical work. Further, our results may serve as a basis to experimentally engineer magnetic domain based quantum networks. Such experiments would enable experimental study on the effects of complex topology on quantum communication networks, a valuable step toward the quantum internet.

title: Acoustic Measures of Prosody in Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract:
Saadia Elahi

Faculty Advisor: Molly Losh, Ph.D.
Doctoral Student Mentor: Shivani Patel, M.A.

Acoustic Measures of Prosody in Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder

Difficulties in social communication are characteristic of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). These difficulties include atypical prosody, or the stress and intonation patterns of speech that are often critical to conveying emotion and intention. Prior work has noted variable prosodic profiles in ASD, such as sounding too monotone or too singsongy, based on listener ratings. To provide objective characterization of prosody in ASD, we assessed acoustic measures of pitch during affect expression (like vs. dislike) and turn-end type expression (statement vs. question production), both of which may negatively impact social interaction if used inappropriately. This study utilized speech samples from the Profiling Elements of Prosody in Speech-Communication (PEPS-C), a task assessing one’s ability to comprehend and produce prosody. Speech analysis software (Praat) was utilized to extract measures of mean, range, and standard deviation of fundamental frequency (F0) in a sample of 14 individuals with ASD and 11 typically developing (TD) controls. Linear mixed effects models, covarying for age and gender, were conducted to assess differences between ASD and TD groups. While no significant group differences emerged on the Turn-End subtest, results revealed significantly lower range of F0 on the Affect subtest in the ASD group, reflecting reduced pitch variability when conveying emotion. As such, reduced pitch variability during affect expression may be an important aspect of atypical prosody contributing to social communication deficits noted in ASD. Future work may seek to assess the utility of targeting pitch modulation to improve affect expression among individuals with ASD.

title: All Roads Lead to Palestine
abstract: All Roads Lead to Palestine is a documentary following three Palestinian families, and the different paths they took to end up in Qatar today. Seeing as Qatar has a large, passionate Palestinian community, and as I am a Palestinian myself, I wanted to learn more about how they perceive their home country, and the reasons they are currently living in Qatar. Therefore, I set out with the goal of creating a short documentary on the Palestinian diaspora in Qatar for my Mobile Journalism class. I contacted various Palestinians with different backgrounds and filmed the interviews using only a mobile phone and a GorillaPod. Then it occurred to me that focusing on different generations within the same families could further provide insight on the varying psychological effects of being part of the diaspora. This documentary showcases the different hardships these Palestinians faced in leaving their country, and how they maintain a strong connection regardless of the distance. It sheds light on their feelings, passions and struggles.

title: Analysis of the CueR Constitutive Activator Variant (CueRCA) through Crystallography and DNA-Binding
abstract: The sensing and regulating of metal ions is crucial for the survival of bacterial organisms such as Escherichia coli. Due to its high toxicity, copper is regulated through a homeostatic copper efflux system. In this system, the CueR protein acts as a transcriptional regulator of two copper efflux genes by distorting DNA upon copper-binding. My project strived to characterize the role of an individual protein domain, the C-terminal helix, in the metal-bound activator conformation of CueR, as it undergoes the induced change for transcriptional activation. To determine this role, a mutant variant of the CueR protein was created that exhibits clear Cu(I)-independent transcription activation (CueRCA) at all copper concentrations. The constitutive activator variant was overexpressed and purified for characterization by Native gel shift assay and crystallography. Crystallization conditions were screened and optimized to produce CueRCA crystals that diffracted to ~2.45 Å. I found that (1) CueRCA does bind to DNAs of different lengths, and (2) all CueR residues are present in the CueRCA structure, except the metal-binding loop (MBL). This supports my hypothesis that the CTH ultimately stabilizes the activator confirmation and that CueRCA superactivation does not result from changes to other residues. The structure of CueRCA has therefore provided evidence of both key details of transcription activation in E. coli and a similar mechanism shared with other metalloregulators and ligand-binding proteins in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. This indicates an approach that has been evolutionarily conserved and remains adaptable to the binding of different ligands with protein/DNA complexes.

title: Anna Amalia: a dramatized case study in the life & legacy of 18th century women composers
abstract: Despite centuries of active participation in the Western musical world, few women are acknowledged as skilled composers. Anna Amalia, a composer from 18th century Prussia, has faded in history, while textbooks fawn over the compositions of her brother, Frederick the Great. Although Princess Amalia’s library of musical scores has proven instrumental to the preservation and study of countless musicians -- the world-renowned J.S. Bach, in particular, -- substantial knowledge of her own life and legacy remains scattered throughout brief footnotes and parenthetical citations. To address such a wide gap in knowledge, this project combined several research methods, ranging from close analysis of biographies of more famous figures from Amalia’s lifetime, to site-specific research of palaces and instrument collections in Berlin, Germany, to creative explorations of Amalia’s surviving musical compositions. These methods culminated in a full length play about Amalia. Although still in development, this play represents a new chapter in the history of plays about musicians: it weaves together music and more-traditional theatrical structures to tell a story on a larger scale than any other play about a woman composer to date. The excerpted scenes presented here explore Amalia’s childhood, as she challenges the patriarchal authority blocking her from following her passion for music. The scenes also provide a snapshot into three other major characters in the play, as they push past their limited agency as young people in order to fight for what they believe in. Follow the continuing journey on instagram: @annaamaliaplay.

title: Are You One of Us? A Qualitative Study of How White Appearing College Students Make Sense of Their Identities, Find Communities, and Interact with Racial and Ethnic Affinity Spaces
abstract: College students of color experience greater harassment and perceive campus climate as more racist and less accepting than their white peers. Racial and ethnic affinity groups aim to provide supports for students of color, but in fact often don’t serve phenotypically ambiguous students. While past research has typically characterized multiracial participants as ambiguous, limited work exists on the identity development and group membership of both monoracial and multiracial white appearing individuals. Even less work focuses on the college context. To address this gap, the present study examines how 10 white appearing college students make sense of their identities and how that understanding informs their experiences finding communities and interacting with racial and ethnic affinity spaces. Using grounded theory to analyze the data from in-person, semi-structured interviews, this study found that white appearing students are often uncertain about their identity and are mainly constructing their racial and ethnic identity via primary caregivers and communities. When seeking communities, they long for acceptance, using their life experiences and performing in ways to justify that their white appearance does not match how they feel. Still, they are rejected by racial and ethnic communities for not being authentic enough. This rejection causes participants to diminish their whiteness and idealize the experiences of people of color as they desire to feel accepted for who they are. Ultimately, most participants leave racial and ethnic communities, finding non-exclusive communities to be more accepting and supportive. These data bring light to how white appearing college students find supports.

title: Assessing the effect of Liposomal Spherical Nucleic Acid stability on Vaccine Function for Triple Negative Breast Cancer
abstract: The successful development of vaccines for triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) has been hindered because there are no identified tumor-associated antigens. As an alternative to peptide vaccines, the administration of tumor lysates has been investigated in TNBC to activate the immune system against tumors, wherein a mixture of tumor-specific lysates is administered to behave as antigens. The Mirkin group has previously demonstrated the capability of Liposomal Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) to initiate antigen presentation and activate immune cells. Liposome SNA’s consist of a concentric phospholipid vesicle core where the adjuvant is anchored into the bilayer, and the lysate is encapsulated within the core. With this novel delivery method in mind, we proposed a two-pronged investigation. First, we assessed whether changing the stability of the SNA impacts antigen delivery, by comparing four different lipid constituents and their decay rate in serum. Second, we investigated whether changing the hydrophobicity of the DNA anchor affected SNA decay rate. From these investigations, we find that SNA stability is governed by both liposome membrane fluidity and anchor hydrophobicity, and that these parameters are additive. Taken together, our findings will be able to significantly optimize the way cancer vaccines for TNBC are designed and administered.

title: Black Queer Women's Articulations of Masculinity & Femininity on YouTube
abstract: While previous black queer and feminist literature has considered how Black people and Black queer women have unique relationships to gender, there is limited sociological work looking at Black queer women’s relationship to gender and the ways that digital technologies mediate this relationship. To address this gap, the current study examines the performative and discursive articulations of masculinity and femininity in Black queer women’s YouTube videos. Thirty-four YouTube videos from Black queer women uploaded between 2016 and 2020 were analyzed for patterns in how gender expression and presentation were discussed across the videos. Findings revealed that (1) the concept of authenticity (i.e., a sense of alignment between the internal desires of one’s body and the presentation of their body) is central to Black queer women’s gendered performances on YouTube and (2) Black queer women use digital media platforms, such as YouTube, to encourage their followers to seek a sense of authenticity and exert bodily autonomy over their self-presentations.

title: Bloom
abstract: I created this sculpture after hearing the song Bloom by Troye Sivan. He sings to a person that makes him bloom, and it made me think about how wonderful it is to find someone who makes you want to bloom, grow and be better for them. But I also think we should be that person for ourselves too. To love and take care of ourselves, that we finally bloom to who we want to be. Mental health is a topic that is very important to me. I have struggled to pull myself out of a dark place and slowly bloom to who I am today. I think it is through being aware and monitoring ourselves that we work on self-love and self-care. It is a process hence, why the sculpture is black, the sculpture or the person it represents, is still in the process of blooming from the darkness to the light or a better version of themselves. To create it, I used my sister’s torso as a model then used newspapers and paper mache to create the sculpture. There are flowers coming out of the sculpture’s head but also a large flower by its heart. Meaning, blooming should not just be in how you think but also in how you feel.

title: BMK-1 provides a redundant sorting force for spindle bipolarity
abstract: The proper development of embryos depends on faithful meiotic chromosome segregation to produce gametes. Failure of proper chromosome segregation results in aneuploidy, or the state of having an irregular number of chromosomes in a cell, which has human health implications due to its potential in causing congenital abnormalities and miscarriages. Though centrosomes are normally involved in cell division, oocytes lack centrosomes and must thus carry out chromosome segregation with acentriolar processes. By using C. elegans to study oocyte meiosis, this research project seeks to understand the motor forces responsible for bipolar spindle organization. Dynein is a motor protein known to sort microtubules with its polar properties, and the depletion of dynein results in splayed spindle poles that are unable to fully join together. When a monopolar spindle is induced by the depletion of the kinesin protein KLP-18, further dynein depletions result in the complete dissolution of the monopole. Interestingly, the resulting individual chromosomes are able to proceed through anaphase without having to first line up in the typical metaphase plate of chromosome segregation. By then depleting the BMK-1 protein simultaneously with both KLP-18 and dynein, we have found that BMK-1 provides a redundant motor force responsible for this spindle reorganization, which is normally undetectable due to the major forces exerted by dynein and KLP-18. Therefore, our studies have furthered the understanding of acentriolar oocyte meiosis and of how multiple motors work synchronously to establish and maintain bipolarity in the absence of centrosomes.

title: Characterization of triclosan tolerance mechanisms across Pseudomonas strains
abstract: The widespread use of triclosan as an antimicrobial agent has led to its dissemination in indoor and outdoor environments. Its presence may select for triclosan tolerance in members of resident microbial communities, including enrichment of the genus Pseudomonas, thereby encompassing potential pathogens. Antimicrobial resistance in Pseudomonas could negatively impact human health outcomes. However, triclosan tolerance mechanisms are not well characterized for Pseudomonas species beyond the well-studied P. aeruginosa. To elucidate the contributions of triclosan-refractory enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductases (ENR) and multidrug efflux in conferring tolerance, Pseudomonas isolates representing multiple strains from indoor dust and hospital sink drains were subjected to transposon mutagenesis and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing for triclosan. A bimodal distribution of high MIC (≥128 mg/L) and low MIC (≤0.5 mg/L) isolates reflected the presence or absence of the FabV isozyme of the ENR, respectively. Among fabV-negative transposon mutants, transposon insertion increased the MIC by upregulating efflux or increasing expression of the FabI isozyme. Among fabV-positive mutants, transposon insertion in efflux pump genes reduced the MIC. Addition of an efflux pump inhibitor reduced but did not eliminate triclosan tolerance for all isolates, further demonstrating reliance on fabV for conferring higher triclosan tolerance. This study demonstrates the universal role of efflux in conferring triclosan tolerance across Pseudomonas species and that presence of fabV predicts high triclosan tolerance. Results expand upon knowledge of triclosan tolerance mechanisms within Pseudomonas species and indicate that a single strain may not be an apt representative for the triclosan tolerance profile of an entire genus.

title: Completing Mahler’s Piano Quartet:  A Study of Unfinished Music, Ethics, and Authenticities
abstract:
Isabella Spinelli
Jesse Rosenberg
Completing Mahler’s Unfinished Piano Quartet: An Investigation of Ethics, Authenticity, and Genius

For generations, performers and scholars have argued over what should be done with musical works that were left incomplete.  Many attempts have been made to bring these works to completion, but some feel that these fragments should remain untouched, mostly because the pieces in question were left incomplete at a height in the composer’s career.  I studied and completed Gustav Mahler’s Piano Quartet in A minor, of which Mahler composed a complete first movement, Nicht zu schnell, and twenty-four bars of a second, Scherzo, when he was a student at the Vienna Conservatory—well before the height of his output.  I began my work by analyzing Nicht zu schnell in order to understand Mahler’s treatment of motives, form, and harmony.  In addition, I studied the Schumann and Brahms piano quartets as Mahler likely did.   I then composed a completion of the Scherzo in a way I felt Mahler may have based on my analysis.  When presenting a performance of the work, I distributed a survey to gage audience member’s reactions.  When asked how closely they found Scherzo to align with Nicht zu schnell, 70% of the audience members responded with fives on a scale of zero to six, and 100% approved of the task of completing unfinished music.  These results demonstrate that, when presented with a completion of a work left unfinished early in a composer’s career, a significant consensus among those who filled out the questionnaire were unconcerned with issues such as genius and hubris, thus confirming my suspicions.

title: Completing Mahler’s Piano Quartet:  A Study of Unfinished Music, Ethics, and Authenticities
abstract:
Description and Artist’s Statement
This completion of Gustav Mahler’s Piano Quartet in A minor, Scherzo, interrogates composers’ intentions, historical style, and the concept of genius.  For generations, performers and scholars have argued over what should be done with musical works that were left incomplete.  Many attempts have been made to bring these works to completion, but these attempts have aroused various kinds of controversy.  As a student at the Vienna Conservatory, Gustav Mahler composed one complete movement, Nicht zu schnell, and twenty-four bars of a second, incomplete movement, Scherzo, of his A minor quartet.  Based on thorough analysis of the first movement as well as chamber music by Robert Schumann and Johannes Brahms that likely served as models for the young Mahler, my completion presents one way in which Mahler may have finished the movement had he continued past bar twenty-four.

title: Compositions exploring comedy and female sexuality. Two songs entitled Hey Mama and Fallin'
abstract: The realm of standup comedy is largely dominated by male sexual bravado. Female comedians who joke about their sexuality face criticism and slut shaming. I set out to explore how bringing comedy and female sexuality into a musical medium could be used as a subversive tool for gender commentary. I read up on gender theory, analyzed female performance, and wrote songs on a variety of topics including hookup culture, forgiving “the other woman,” and finding fulfilment as a woman in ways other than relationally. I learned that singing can lead an audience to be more forgiving to humor that might be considered abrasive for women in other contexts. I also learned that it’s difficult to overcome the double standards I’ve internalized and to push myself out of my comedic comfort zone. The songs I’ve written are continuously being developed and continue to necessitate the right occasion for performance. The niche of musical comedy relating to femininity has very rich potential for expression and I will continue to compose in this avenue and argue for its importance.

title: Computer-assisted snowball search for meta-analysis research
abstract: The rapidly increasing number of publications in the clinical sciences presents both new opportunities and challenges for meta-analysis research. While this has allowed more robust evaluations of diagnoses and interventions, there are now more papers that the researcher must find, screen, and analyze. This is not to be underestimated: the PRISMA guideline for systematic literature review recommends a comprehensive database search which involves following the citations and references from a starting set of core articles to find related articles and repeating the process for the newly found articles to collect primary data sources relevant to the research question. This process, called “snowball search,” has traditionally been done largely by hand, limiting the scale and scope of meta-analysis research. However, recent growths in online databases and calls for open access have made scholarly databases more available to individual researchers, providing potential for the search process to be automated. We report on the performance and design philosophy of our tool Snowballer, a software for conducting automatic searches for citations and references, developed in collaboration with meta-analysis researchers in child language development. Snowballer uses a downloadable snapshot of the open-source Microsoft Academic database to find a paper’s citations and references and sends queries across multiple online databases to fetch information about the searched papers that can help facilitate the screening process. Findings from a pilot and a validation experiment demonstrate the potential for automated approaches to significantly reduce resource barriers to meta-analysis research without compromising a representative coverage of the target literature.

title: Creating Equity: Stakeholders’ Perceptions of an Equity Initiative in a California School District
abstract: This study examined stakeholders’ perceptions of SPARK, an equity initiative, in two historically underserved elementary schools in California. It analyzed 31 interview transcripts to uncover variation in the content and manner of perceptions both between and within three organizational levels: teachers, school leaders, and district leaders. This research is novel in its comparison of perceptions of an equity reform between organizational levels. The study found considerable confusion about SPARK at each level of organization and highlighted strong differences in perceptions of SPARK between the two schools. The results of this study offer a more nuanced understanding of stakeholders’ perceptions, which suggest that in order for new equity initiatives to be successful they must involve a clear design of the initiative with concrete goals and strategies and they must be accompanied by frequent and truthful communication of information and perceptions of the initiative between stakeholders.

title: Dendritic Spinule Dynamics, Regulation, and Function
abstract: Dendritic spines are neuronal structures known to be involved in synaptic plasticity, connectivity, and communication. Disruptions in spine shape, size, and number may contribute to the development of neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease and schizophrenia. Spinules are thin dendritic spine protrusions, and can be small, transient, and motile, or elongated and stabilized by contacting other neuronal elements. These protrusions are often induced and enhanced by neuronal activity and are commonly found in healthy brain tissue. However, how spinule morphology and dynamics relate to their function and role in neuropsychiatric disease are unknown. Neurons from a mouse model were chemically transfected with various fluorescent proteins and plasmids. FM dyes were used to label presynaptic terminals of axons, a possible contact for dendritic spinules. These techniques were performed for future fluorescent imaging and visualization of the neuron cultures. High-speed 3D structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and enhanced resolution confocal microscopy were used to image the neuronal cultures and observe spinule dynamics and morphology over time. The data reveals that there are two classes of spinules: short-lived and long-lived. Induced neuronal activation increased spinule number per spine and contacts with distal neuronal elements. Specifically, activity-induced, long-lived spinules extend towards and contact presynaptic terminals, and this may play a role in secondary synapse formation. The data suggest that spinules may facilitate neuronal connectivity, and that spinule dysfunction may be associated with neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Design, synthesis, and evaluation of natural product-inspired small molecules targeting the serotonin-2C receptor
abstract: Understimulation of the serotonin-2c receptor in the central nervous system has been strongly linked to neurological disorders ranging from opioid addiction to schizophrenia in mice models. Designing a small molecule agonist which upregulates the 2c pathway could prove to be a useful clinical angle in tackling maladaptive behaviors faced by growing segments of the populace. However, the serotonin-2a receptor, a receptor with a similarly-configured binding site for serotonin is known to cause cardiovascular abnormalities when overstimulated by synthetic agonists, molecules that mimic the structure and function of serotonin. Agonists therefore need to be potent and selective for 2c. Starting from yohimbine alkaloids, a class of compounds isolated from the Rauvolfia vomitoria plant, molecules were designed using computational models and synthesized in-house using Pictet-Spengler condensations. These compounds were high-throughput screened using in vitro Ca2+-flux assays and tested on mice models. Preliminary data on ortho-substituted analogs have indicated good binding efficacy and selectivity. One such compound reported has <10nM EC50 and a 6.5 selectivity 2c/2a in vitro, measurables approaching Lorcaserin, the only FDA-approved drug for the 2c receptor to date. Further modifications and improvements to ortho-functionalized analogs are expected to be the next step in optimizing the functional selectivity of serotonin analogs as a potential market pharmaceutical.

title: Developing Special Protection Mechanisms for Female Journalists in Colombia
abstract: Colombian journalist Jineth Bedoya was kidnapped on May 25, 2000 when covering a prison riot in Bogotá. Held hostage for 16 hours, the journalist was repeatedly raped and tortured in response to her journalistic work. Due to its level of brutality and impunity, Bedoya’s story has become emblematic in Colombia. Yet, hers is not an isolated case; it is instead the reflection of a systemic issue in a country historically affected by different forms of violence. As a response to the lack of action by the Colombian State, in 2019, her case was submitted to the highest international court in the Americas: the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, representing the first case to address the intersection of violence against women and the press at the Court. In that sense, the journalist not only finally has an opportunity to push for the implementation of effective protective and compensatory measures after twenty years of impunity, but the Court can rule on the rights of female journalists, setting a precedent not only for Colombia but for the Americas. I have investigated how past Court rulings have facilitated the implementation of good practices throughout the Americas. Based on that, my research advocates for the implementation of mechanisms focused on measures of prevention, protection, and prosecution (PPP) related to violence against female journalists. Since around 43% of the region’s journalists identify as women, Jineth Bedoya et al. v. Colombia will set the precedent for nearly half of the communicators in the Americas.

title: Development of an Improved Orthogonal Ribosome
abstract: A core goal of synthetic biology has been the evolution of macromolecular machines for compelling societal and scientific applications. Specifically, there has been significant interest in using directed evolution to engineer the ribosome for making new medicines and materials. Here we present our approach and progress in engineering the ribosome, which overcome previous hurdles in ribosome engineering. Integrating cutting­ edge computational RNA design of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) into the design­ build test cycle and using both in vivo and in vitro experimental platforms for ribosome synthesis and evolution, we modify and evolve the ribosome in ways previously intractable. Using our approach, we developed Ribo­T v3, a new and improved version of the tethered ribosome with an over 50% improvement in orthogonal protein translation. To evolve Ribo­ for improved function, we demonstrate the use of Rosetta­ guided design in iterative evolution experiments, and a new technique termed Evo­link (evolution and linkage of distant regions). Evo­link allows for the high-throughput evolution of functionally linked regions that are distal in primary sequence but close in 3D space by coupling flexible molecular biology techniques with next­-generation sequencing. Our work demonstrates the power of computational structural modeling for informing library design, and the potential of high­ throughput experimentation (Evo­link, cell­free ribosome assembly and translation) to optimize macromolecular machines for applications in energy, materials, and medicine.

title: Developments or Division? The Role Large Public Investment Project Plays in Gentrification: A Case Study on Chicago’s 606 Bloomingdale Bike Trail
abstract: Efficiency and equity have always been the key dilemma in local economic developments. On the one hand, economic prosperity is crucial for sustainable growth; on the other hand, the neighborhoods might undergo gentrification, transforming the area to appeal to high-end markets. Hence, vulnerable or indigenous residents might face displacements, and the neighborhood would lose its originality and authenticity. This thesis project takes a quantitative approach by using the difference-in-differences method to examine hybrid form of gentrification in modern American cities. Specifically, the research narrows its lens on the 606 Bloomingdale Bike Trail in Chicago to gain generalized insights for these newly formed rail-to-trail projects. In order to examine the treatment of this bike trail, Chicago census data from 2010 to 2017 is collected and divided into two groups: one that is within a mile of the bike trail and one that is not. Findings only partially support my hypotheses. They show that gentrification is rather exacerbating segregation within the community, instead of converting the disinvested neighborhoods. The bike trail fortifies the barriers to live in the wealthier regions while continuing to isolate the disinvested parts. Results also suggest that, in the case of the 606, gentrification is actually resisting changes that happened over time in other Chicago areas. Further research using spatial regression is required to determine the extent and the composition of the 606’s effect on its surrounding neighborhoods.

title: Diet Effects on the Non-Human Primate Gut Microbiome
abstract: With concerns about how to feed an exponentially growing, increasingly obese population, humanity’s relationship with food is a pressing concern. Evaluating the evolutionary changes in the composition of gut microbiota (GM), defined as the microorganisms that live in the digestive tract, may offer insight into how human bodies have adapted to these changing metabolic and energetic needs. Host diet has proven to influence the composition and function of the GM, which subsequently affects human nutrition and health via interactions with metabolism, the immune system, and brain. Due to the lack of ancient human soft tissue, nonhuman primates (NHPs) can be used to understand the GM’s presumed role in initiating changes in human metabolic pathways over time, particularly in response to a shift from a low fat high fiber diet (LFHF) to a high fat low fiber diet (HFLF). My project investigated if the primate GM changes in response to an industrialized, HFLF diet by focusing on the fecal samples of 2 different populations of wild baboons in Rwanda’s Alkagera National Park, one that eats a LFHF diet and the other that eats a HFLF diet. By conducting 16s rRNA bacterial gene sequencing, preliminary data indicates that diet strongly impacts GM composition, and that baboons consuming a HFLF diet have reduced microbial diversity. Because current literature focuses on clinical scenarios, or has captivity as a confounding variable, this work contributes to limited data on host-microbe relationships in wild NHPs that can inform how a long-term HFLF diet impacts human physiology.

title: Digital Diplomacy during the first 100 Days
abstract: This research focuses on the different ways the Ministries of foreign Affairs and Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the GCC have used Twitter as an instrument of digital diplomacy during the first 100 days of the Blockade.

title: Dismantling Voluntourism: Evaluating the Effects of a Global Health Supplemental Curriculum on Undergraduate Volunteers Travelling to Haiti
abstract:
In the era of international volunteerism, mounting evidence suggests that the presence of unskilled and culturally unaware volunteers in the Global South fosters “voluntourism”, and endangers the very populations and institutions that volunteers want to help. Northwestern does not enforce a pre-trip curriculum for student organizations that coordinate private service trips, leaving the students to independently prepare themselves for their trip. This spring, eight students including myself intended to volunteer in Haiti through a Haitian-based non-profit, coordinated by a Northwestern student organization. Taking this opportunity, I implemented an eight-week pre-departure global health/ethics curriculum, and assessed the students to determine if a supplemental curriculum was effective in establishing competency in global health, ethical service, and Haitian history/culture. Students were evaluated through qualitative methods and quantitative evaluations. This study found that the curriculum was sufficient in establishing cultural sensitivity, historical awareness, and basic global health/ethics competency. Students also developed a critical lens of service in the Global South, and heightened awareness of how their privilege would affect their engagement in Haiti. Students preferred a supplemental curriculum to a for-credit class, and cited their schedules as barriers to taking global health classes or choosing university-sponsored international programs. Participants admitted that without the curriculum, they would not have individually sought out this information. The results of this study suggest that a country-specific supplemental curriculum is effective in creating a cohort of culturally and ethically sensitive student volunteers, and should be a minimum requirement for undergraduate service efforts in the Global South.

Faculty Advisor: Peter Locke

title: Does This Look Okay, Mom? — Mother-Daughter Interactions with Body Image
abstract: Negative body image in women has been a prevalent issue throughout history. Societal expectations have left many women feeling insecure and dissatisfied. Current research has indicated that oftentimes negative body image is passed down from mother to daughter. While there is a variety of research on mother-daughter interactions with body image, there is not a lot of research that specifically studies the connotation of words used.  This research explored the correlation between body satisfaction among mothers and daughters, the correlation between connotation of words used by mothers and daughters’ body satisfaction, and cultural norms surrounding mother-daughter interactions with body image. In an online survey, college women (n=100) were asked to report body satisfaction of their mothers, personal body satisfaction, perceived language mothers used to describe their own appearance and daughters’ appearances, and cultural norms surrounding these interactions. It was hypothesized that there would be a positive correlation between mother and daughter body satisfaction which was confirmed by the results. Overall, daughters reported more negative words used by their mothers to describe their own appearance and more positive words used by their mothers to describe daughters’ appearances. There is a positive correlation between daughters’ body satisfaction and number of positive words used by mothers to describe daughters. Also, Asian/Asian-American women reported that it was more common in their culture for mothers to critique their appearance. These findings are limited due to self-reported and perceived data but encourage further research on the role of language on body image particularly among familial relationships.

title: Doubly Burdened, Dually Strained:  The Strategic Utilization of Chicago’s Community Health Workers in Task-Shifting Interventions
abstract: Drawing on ethnographic research approaches including semi-structured qualitative interviews and participant-observation, in this thesis I examine how Black and Latina Community Health Workers (CHWs) in Chicago navigate their mandate to influence peer health behaviors and build bridges with underserved groups. Often associated with settings of poverty and limited infrastructure in the Global South, CHW programs—a mode of “task-shifting” key health care services from specialists to less expensive labor—are increasingly implemented as a possible solution to persistent and acute health disparities in the metropolises of the Global North. Because CHWs are active members of the community in which they serve, they provide a crucial link between health providers and those communities that face barriers to clinical space. This is especially true in communities where histories of abuse and mistrust define the provider-patient relationship. This thesis demonstrates that CHWs’ identities as members of these marginalized communities play an important role in how they approach their mission and complicates reductive visions of CHWs harmoniously disseminating information, increasing healthcare use, and re-forging relations of trust between health systems and vulnerable people. The CHWs I encountered struggled with tensions between local knowledge and values and the burden of increasing the utilization of systems that they know to be flawed and unequal, underscoring that task-shifting is no magic bullet for inequalities with complex and long-standing determinants. I use these findings to call into question the potentials and limitations of CHW programs, highlighting the counter-intuitive positionalities that pull at either end of community identity and workforce expectations. This study contributes to the ongoing discussion of dissemination of health information to underserved populations and provides recommendations for more effective implementation of task-shifting approaches in the future.

title: Effects of Hearing Loss on Selective Attention from Childhood to Adulthood
abstract: Listeners have difficulty understanding speech in environments containing background noise. This difficulty is exacerbated for listeners with hearing loss, which is often attributed to the degradation of the speech signal caused by interfering noise, impaired hearing, hearing device processing, or a combination of these factors. To resolve and understand speech despite this degradation, listeners must allocate attention to the speech signal and inhibit their attention to competing background noise. Thus, the inability to selectively attend to speech is expected to reduce speech recognition. Consistent with this idea is the observation that selective auditory attention is poorer in children with hearing loss, and these abilities partially account for children’s difficulty understanding speech in background noise. However, it remains unknown whether the effects of hearing loss on selective attention persist into adulthood and, if so, whether this contributes to the speech recognition difficulties of young adults with hearing loss. The present study aimed to address the first of these knowledge gaps by having young adults with hearing loss and normal hearing perform selective attention tasks in the auditory and visual domains. Young adults with hearing loss demonstrated similar selective attention to their peers with normal hearing in the visual domain, but not in the auditory domain. This latter finding, however, may have been related to poor audibility among the hearing loss group. The data support the idea that audibility is important for selective auditory attention in adults.

title: Elucidation and Development of Synthetic Receptor Mechanisms for Sensing Protein Ligands
abstract: Cell-based therapies are a promising technology for treating diseases, with approved clinical applications such as cancer immunotherapy. Such therapies necessitate the development of custom sense-and-respond functionality to extend cells’ ability to target specific physiological environments and disease states. To achieve this, synthetic receptors, such as Modular Extracellular Sensor Architecture (MESA), have been engineered to sense soluble ligands and cell surface markers. In MESA, each receptor comprises two transmembrane proteins that heterodimerize upon ligand binding to initiate intracellular signaling linked to downstream transcriptional outputs. Such biosensors rewire detection of extracellular ligands to production of a therapeutic protein. As with other engineered receptor systems, translation of MESA receptors to sense new targets of interest poses many challenges. Notably, many physiologically-relevant proteins like cytokines are typically multimeric in nature and much larger than small molecules sensed in model systems. Here, towards the goal of engineering versatile biosensors, dimerization propensities of MESA receptors are characterized using Förster resonance energy transfer, providing insights about receptor geometry for ligands of varying size. Building on these characterizations, a new MESA receptor mechanism that aims to overcome the identified challenges is explored. This new receptor design incorporates pre-formed receptor complexes that inhibit ligand-independent background signaling and receptor activation via the binding of large ligands that separate these pre-formed inhibitory complexes, enabling signaling. This new mechanism is tailored for large ligand targets and amenable to binding homodimeric ligands. This investigation has identified required features for engineered receptors to sense protein-based ligands and expands the therapeutic potential of cell-based therapies.

title: Exploring the Detection of Missing Tissue in Planarian Regeneration
abstract: Animals can heal minor injuries, but severe wounds often result in the production of scar tissue. However, some animals can replace lost tissues in a specialized process called regeneration. Schmidtea mediterranea, a planarian flatworm, is a promising model organism for the study of regeneration due to its extensive repair abilities. Planaria can heal after a wide variety of wounds, but the mechanisms that differentiate between injuries that require simple healing and those that require regeneration remain poorly understood. All injuries activate characteristic transcriptional and cellular responses, but these responses are sustained only if tissue is removed by injury. Therefore, it is likely that some unknown signal either induced by or concomitant with tissue loss activates the sustained “missing tissue response” to promote regeneration. To identify this signal, I screened for factors that activate follistatin, a gene whose expression is sustained after tissue loss and initiates the missing tissue response. After silencing the expression of a set of candidate genes, I assessed the level of follistatin expression after injury. Silencing bmp, smad1, and smad4, three members of the BMP signaling pathway, resulted in a failure to activate wound-induced follistatin expression and regeneration defects. This indicates that BMP signaling, which establishes dorsoventral identity in planaria, is involved in sensing tissue loss. Therefore, I propose that contact between dorsal and ventral tissues during wound closure signals that tissue has been lost. Understanding how planaria sense and respond to tissue damage will contribute to fundamental knowledge about the mechanisms that initiate and promote regeneration.

title: Exploring the Effects of Phonetic Overlap and Background Noise on Incremental Processing in Children
abstract: In everyday conversation, individuals actively process speech in order to comprehend and respond in real-time. As a word unfolds, listeners activate possible lexical candidates and actively determine the target word as they receive more information, a process referred to as incremental processing. This process requires knowledge of one’s native spoken language and the ability to recognize individual phonemes. While this process allows for rapid word recognition, it can also result in phonological competition among multiple candidate words that have phonetic overlap. This has been shown for words that share the same initial phonemes (e.g., candle and candy). However, other types of phonetic overlap, such as rhyme (e.g., candle and sandal), are not well explored. The present study implemented an eye-tracking paradigm in school-age children to quantify incremental language processing of words that rhyme with or share offset phonetic information with other words. The experimental method enabled us to measure the extent to which children looked at target images (e.g., candle) as well as images that served as rhyme competitors (e.g., sandal), shared offset competitors (e.g., poodle), and unrelated distractors (e.g, diaper) as the target speech unfolded. Children completed the task in quiet as well as in the presence of broadband background noise, which disrupts the acoustic representation of the speech input. The data suggest that phonetic overlap does impact incremental processing in quiet. However, the background noise condition slows processing speed to a certain extent for each of the three competitor image condition.

title: Exploring the Relationship between Children’s Life Stories and the Big Five Personality Traits
abstract: Life stories are strong predictors of identity, since the specific narratives adults tell about themselves represent individual differences in personality characteristics. One way researchers analyze these life stories in adults is by measuring the story’s coherence, which is comprised of a clear context, a linear chronology, and an explanation of why the specified events are important to the narrator. In doing so, researchers have found that more coherent personal narratives are related to better memory and communication, and stronger understandings of one’s own identity. In the present study, I explored the relationship between narrative coherence and personality traits in children in an effort to examine children’s ability to tell life stories and how those stories relate to their developing identities. Participants were 367 children (53.1% female) ages 9-14 (Mage = 12.1, SD = 0.80). Children’s best and sad memories were coded for coherence, whereupon I analyzed whether the Five-Factor Model personality traits were associated with more coherent narratives. I also sought to determine whether Coherence was associated with age and gender. Results revealed that Sad Memory Coherence was generally unassociated with personality traits. However, Best Memory Coherence demonstrated some associations with Neuroticism, Openness, and Extraversion. These were variable across measures. Additionally, while age was unassociated with most coherence dimensions, gender was found to associate with most dimensions of coherence, such that girls’ best and sad memories were generally rated as more coherent than were boys’. While these are only preliminary results, they provide important insight into identity development in children.

title: Facial Expressions in Adolescent-Parent Interactions and Links with Anxiety and Depression: A Dyadic Approach
abstract: Close relationships play a key role in mental health, and facial expressions are important social signals in our interactions. Few studies have examined facial expressions of emotion and links with anxiety and depression in adolescent-parent interactions, which may be crucibles for mental health development. Drawing from affective, developmental, and clinical science frameworks, the present laboratory-based study used a dyadic approach to examine facial expressions of emotion (objectively measured on a frame-by-frame basis) during conflict, pleasant, and neutral adolescent-parent interactions (each lasting 10 minutes) and links with anxiety and depressive symptoms (each measured in both adolescents and parents). A total of 2,490,000 video frames across 1,660 video minutes in 28 adolescent-parent dyads were analyzed using actor-partner interdependence modeling. Results revealed that (a) adolescents’ neutral expressions were positively associated with adolescents’ and parents’ anxiety and depression, (b) parents’ negative expressions were positively associated with adolescents’ and parents’ anxiety and depression, and (c) adolescents’ happy expressions were negatively associated with parents’ anxiety and depression (although this association was not robust when controlling for demographic variables). Results largely generalized across the three interaction contexts (conflict, pleasant, and neutral). Together, these results suggest the utility of facial expressions (neutral expressions for adolescents, negative expressions for parents) as behavioral markers of psychopathology, emphasize the importance of adolescent-parent interactions for anxiety and depression, and suggest directions for future affective, developmental, and clinical research.

title: Family Environment and Brain Structure Interact to Predict  Depressive Symptoms in Trauma-Exposed Girls
abstract: While it is well-understood that exposure to trauma increases one’s risk of developing depression, a growing body of evidence suggests that this relationship can be either intensified or mitigated by the quality of one’s familial environment. Findings, however, remain inconsistent. One potential explanation is that individuals may differ in their biological sensitivity to environmental context. This study aimed to explore this possibility by examining structural differences in the right Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) as a potential moderator of the association between family climate, parenting practices, and depressive symptoms in trauma-exposed girls. Initial findings showed that family climate and parenting practices were related to depression: girls with more chaotic, enmeshed, and disengaged families reported more depressive symptoms, as did those with poorer parental monitoring and more inconsistent discipline. Conversely, family flexibility and cohesion, as well as parental involvement and positive parenting, were negatively associated with these symptoms. Further analysis revealed that gray matter volume of the right caudal ACC moderated the respective associations between depressive symptoms and family flexibility, family cohesion, and positive parenting. In particular, girls with larger right caudal ACCs showed significantly stronger negative relationships between flexibility and depressive symptoms, cohesion and depressive symptoms, and positive parenting and depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that ACC structure may play a role in modulating sensitivity to familial context. More broadly, they emphasize the importance of considering both biology and environmental context, as well as the complex interplay between the two, when studying trauma resilience and the development of depression.

title: Fractured
abstract:
Description
This short film Fractured was a project for my Docufiction class in which we were tasked to make a personal film. For my personal film I chose to document my struggle with trying to remember the events after a car accident I was involved in. With the amnesia I experienced, I trace back my footsteps trying to fill the blanks. I express what it feels like to live with no memory of the incident and how it affects me mentally and physically to this day.

Artist statement 
Fractured showcases the struggle I face coping with the lack of memory and the physical and mental changes I experience after a life altering car accident. Almost 10 years on, I still try to piece together what happened from fragmented memories, some of which are fact and some fiction. Fractured aims to try and make the audience evoke the same feelings I have surrounding this traumatic incident. I do this by the lack of music, monochromatic theme and softly spoken words.

title: General and Pathological Personality Traits Overlap Substantially in Children and Teens
abstract:
While personality disorders are diagnosed as categorical syndromes, researchers have 
begun to conceptualize personality disorders as extreme variations of general personality traits. Much evidence supports this hypothesis in adults, but no research has yet tested the relationship between “normal” and “abnormal” traits in children. This study explored this relationship using data collected from 1,370 parent reports of personality in children aged 6 to 17 (Mage=10.1 SD=± 3.36) via short­form questionnaires derived from the Inventory of Individual Child Differences (ICID­-S) and the Dimensional Personality Symptom Item Pool (DIPSI­-SF). Four higher order domains of neuroticism, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and extraversion were scored from the ICID­-S item responses and were hypothesized to correlate significantly with the corresponding DIPSI­-SF dimensions of emotional instability, disagreeableness, compulsivity, and introversion respectively based on prior evidence in adults. Results indicated significant, positive correlations between the ICID­S domain of Neuroticism and the DIPSI­-SF domain of Emotional Instability (r =0.689, p<0.001) and the ICID­S domain of Conscientiousness and the DIPSI­-SF Compulsivity domain (r =0.270, p<0.001). A significant, negative correlation was found between the ICID-­S domain of Agreeableness and the DIPSI-­SF domain of Disagreeableness (r =­0.706, p<0.001), and, surprisingly, no significant correlation was found between the domains of Introversion and Extraversion. Additionally, exploratory analysis of a shared psychoticism dimension did not reveal significant overlap between Openness to Experience and Paranoid Traits. These findings suggest a convergence of measures of personality pathology and normative traits in youth on some common, well ­established domains and call for further exploration of this shared dimensional model.

title: Good News and Bad News: College Students' Perceptions of the Political News Media
abstract: Developments in news regulation and business practice over the past several decades have led to an increasingly polarized news media. Recent rhetoric regarding “fake news” has further exacerbated growing mistrust in the media among the American public. Meanwhile, as Generation Z comes of age, tech-literate and social media savvy voters have begun to enter the electorate, begging the question of how they receive and consider political news. Through the qualitative analysis of a dataset of interviews with undergraduate students (n=12), this study discusses the news habits, perceptions, and preferences of a young generation of voters as they navigate this era’s challenges associated with staying informed. Participants’ trust in news publications, in part determined by their own political affiliation, was found to be connected to the reputation of an outlet’s partisan biases. Further, dismay over the perceived increase of biased political commentary in reporting has eroded trust in many news outlets, despite the appeal of eye-catching and entertaining opinion segments. Meanwhile, Twitter has emerged as a dominant news aggregator for social media users. Such findings may be used to better inform news organizations and political campaigns about the desires of their younger audiences, and the broad implications that distrust in the media may have on political discourse and polarization.

title: Habit Strength, Medication Adherence, and Habit-Based Mobile Health Interventions Across Chronic Medical Conditions: Systematic Review
abstract: Unintentional medication nonadherence is common and has been associated with poor health outcomes with increased health care costs. Previous research examined habit’s direct effect on adherence and interactions with factors that influence or overrule it. However, the relationship between habit and adherence, and the role of habit-based mobile health (mHealth) interventions, remains unclear. This review aimed to systematically evaluate the most recent evidence for habit strength, medication adherence, and habit-based mHealth interventions across chronic medical conditions. A keyword search was performed on the PubMed database, and abstract and full-text screening was conducted. PRISMA guidelines were followed when reporting evidence. Of the 687 records examined, 11 met the predefined inclusion criteria and were finalized for data extraction, grading, and synthesis. Most included studies were cross-sectional, used a theoretical model, and measured habit strength using the self-report habit index and self-report behavioral automaticity index. Habit strength was positively correlated with medication adherence in most studies. Habit mediated the effects of self-efficacy on medication adherence, and social norms moderated the effects of habit strength on medication adherence. Habit strength also moderated the effects of poor mental health symptoms and medication adherence. None of the included studies used or proposed a habit-based mHealth behavioral intervention to promote medication adherence. Overall, stronger habit was associated with higher medication adherence, regardless of theoretical model and/or guiding framework. Habit-based interventions should be used to increase medication adherence, and these interventions could leverage widely available mobile technology tools, such as mobile apps or text messaging, and/or existing routines.

title: High On Your Own Supply: Historiographical Analysis of the Literature on Opium Use and Addiction in Southeast Asia
abstract: It is no secret that Southeast Asia has long been a major source of opium production, providing a lucrative enterprise for European empires in the 19th-­20th century. The “Golden Triangle” region, where Myanmar, Laos and Thailand’s borders meet has been one of the world’s largest opium producers since the 1950s. Much has been written in Southeast Asian history about the economic and political impact of opium production in the region, but what of the human cost of addiction, ostracization, and long­term health risks to Southeast Asians? My research sought to present a historiographic analysis of sixteen works on opium in Southeast Asia, spanning from the early 20th century, until today. The results showed that despite a plethora of scholarship on the topic, a miniscule amount of research has been done on the impact of opium use and addiction on Southeast Asians. This  is perhaps due to language barriers, and the obstacles  of a lack of testimony from the most marginalized in society and in sorting through untraditional primary sources where the scars of addiction would be present. As Historian John Smail argued in 1961, it is imperative to start writing autonomous histories of Southeast Asia, looking at sources from the ground, and not from a foreign gunship or merchant house. My historiographic research contributes to an ongoing attempt to critically engage with traditional Euro­centric sources and paradigms, and to start writing the histories of those who never had a voice, casualties of the time perhaps, but not necessarily of history.

title: How Does Adult Attachment Style Relate to Inflammation?
abstract: Anxious and avoidant attachment style in adulthood has been predictive of higher levels of stress, and poor physical and mental health, while secure attachment style serves as a protective factor (e.g., Mikulincer & Shaver, 2012; Pietromonaco, Uchino, & Schetter, 2013). Stress can induce elevated inflammation, a biological risk for physical and mental health (Nusslock & Miller, 2016). The two literatures point to the possibility of a relationship between attachment style and inflammation. However, research examining this question is sparse. To address the literature gap, we explored the relations of several attachment dimensions with inflammation. We hypothesized that anxious and avoidant attachment would associate with higher inflammation while secure attachment would associate with lower inflammation. Method: We recruited 210 older adolescents (M age = 18.6 years; range = 18-19 years) from the Chicago and Los Angeles metropolitan areas. Blood was collected via antecubital venipuncture and assayed for the inflammatory proteins of the interleukin class (IL-6, -8, -10), tumor necrosis-alpha, and C-reactive protein. Inflammatory dynamic was indexed by an inflammation composite score (ICS) from the markers based on the procedure by Nusslock et al. (2019). Measures of attachment quality included the Experience in Close Relationships Questionnaire (Fraley, Waller, & Brennan, 2000) and the Measurement of Attachment Quality (Carver, 1997). Results: In a single linear model, we entered each attachment style as a predictor of the ICS, covarying for the effects of variables known to account for variation in the immune response (e.g., sex, BMI, recent illness). Anxious, avoidant, and secure attachment style did not account for significant variation in the ICS (Mean β = |.07|, ps ≥ .13). Conclusions: Collectively, these results extend our understanding of the cross-sectional relations between adult attachment style and inflammatory activity and partially align with the results of related inquiries (Kidd et al., 2014).

title: Human Laboratory Investigation of Tobacco Withdrawal and Smoking Relapse in Smokers with and without Major Depression
abstract: Smokers with major depressive disorder (MDD) are more susceptible to tobacco dependence and experience more difficulty quitting than those without MDD. Within this high tobacco burden population, the process of tobacco withdrawal and implications for smoking relapse have been reported in epidemiologic studies, but there has been little experimental research. This study sought to investigate affective and cognitive symptoms of tobacco withdrawal in MDD. Data were analyzed from a laboratory study that manipulated withdrawal in adult smokers with and without MDD. Participants abstained from smoking for 48 hours (confirmed using breath carbon monoxide ≤10 ppm) and completed questionnaires assessing affective and cognitive withdrawal symptoms at baseline while smoking as usual and again after 48 hours of abstinence. Participants were re-contacted at 1 month to assess their abstinence status. Participants included 32 smokers, 19 with MDD (MDD+) and 13 without MDD (MDD-), with a mean age of 37.5 (SD=12.0). Compared with MDD- smokers, MDD+ smokers showed significantly greater changes in both affective and cognitive dimensions of withdrawal. By one month, 84.6% of MDD+ smokers relapsed compared to 52.6% of MDD- smokers. This study is the first to distinguish and compare affective and cognitive symptom response to acute abstinence among smokers with MDD and explore the implications for relapse. Although preliminary, greater relapse for MDD smokers may be due to greater overall severity of withdrawal as opposed to greater severity in depression-related withdrawal symptoms. Further experimental research is needed to better understand how acute withdrawal may undermine quitting for MDD smokers.

title: I Am More
abstract:
Abstract

This short documentary shares the story of two housemaids (Hawa Zawadi & Gloria Cortez), in the Middle East who, in an attempt to have a better future, use their free time wisely to practice their hobbies. The documentary covers a series of topics including Zawadi and Cortez’s personal backgrounds, the struggles they face on a daily basis and most importantly, their hobbies outside their working space. They explain the philosophy behind taking such drastic measures to ensure the livelihood to a better future and reveal that working as a housemaid is not an obstacle, but rather a challenge that pushes them to their limitations to fight for their future. They discuss the significance of their hobbies and how they always manage to put some time aside for fun and skill development to draw the right path to their dreams. Finally, they express their emotions about how not letting go of their goals under hard conditions, makes them feel stronger and hopeful whenever they feel that life is falling apart.

Artist Statement

My short documentary offers a unique insight into a much-debated social issue that is prevalent in the Middle East; the issue of housemaids. Through a series of interviews with two housemaids currently working in the Middle East, my documentary looks to showcase the true significance of this often overlooked job. Therefore, by looking at two happy souls, who must resort to creative means to help them endure the hardships that come along with the life of a housemaid in the Middle East, this film seeks to achieve two goals. One, it attempts to empower housemaids all over the Middle East by giving them an opportunity to freely express themselves through sharing different hobbies that they do other than work. Two, this documentary also serves a piece of advice to all women, in that tells them that limitations are just constraints that people create to not only make themselves feel superior, but to also make others feel inferior.

title: Identifying Potential Protein Targets of BET Inhibitors in Enhancing Protein Folding
abstract: As life expectancy increases, humans face considerable health problems due to risk factors for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Diseases. These diseases are associated with an accumulation of protein aggregation in neuronal cells due to protein misfolding and a subsequent decline in quality control. A major cellular protective mechanism regulating protein folding is the heat shock response (HSR). During cellular stress, the transcription factor Heat Shock Factor 1 (HSF1) activates a stress response which induces the expression of chaperone proteins aiding in the refolding of misfolded proteins and alleviating protein aggregation.
