Previously, a small molecule screen was performed employing a human cell line expressing a metastable luciferase folding sensor that misfolds during heat stress. The screen identified several BET (Bromodomain and Extra-Terminal domain) inhibitors that enhanced protein folding. Among the BET protein family, three candidates are known to directly interact with the HSF1 pathway: BRD4; EP300; and GCN5. To understand the mechanism of BET inhibitors in protein folding, human HAP1 (near-haploid) knock out (KO) cell lines of EP300, BRD4, or GCN5 containing a metastable luciferase folding sensor were used to quantify protein folding by luciferase assay. The results show reduced luciferase folding in the BRD4 and EP300 KO cell lines indicating they are regulated by HSF1. Identifying the target will allow for the design of higher potency and specificity of the small molecules to enhance protein folding, providing mechanistic insight into future therapeutics for treating neurodegenerative diseases.

title: In-Vivo Effect of IL-2 Immune Complex on the Progression of Rheumatoid Arthritis
abstract: The goal of this project was to better understand the pathogenesis behind rheumatoid arthritis(RA), an autoimmune disorder that primarily affects the joints. Despite affecting around 1.3 million people in the United States, its causes are not well­-understood. Previous research at Pope Lab indicated that when compared to the healthy controls, the knock­out HUPO mouse model displayed significantly decreased regulatory T cells (Tregs). This deficiency, however, could be restored in­-vitro via administration of recombinant IL­-2. When IL-­2 was bound by its monoclonal antibody, the resulting complex (IL­-2C) had even higher biological activity. Because Tregs generally act to suppress autoreactive T cells that can lead to inflammation, a symptom of RA, the effect of stimulating Treg differentiation through IL-­2C on RA severity was investigated. Both HUPO and control mice with mild RA­like symptoms were chosen and received either PBS, PAP or IL­-2C treatment on an established schedule. Clinical score was assessed weekly to track changes. Half of the mice was harvested at week 3, and the remaining at week 6 for flow cytometry and ankle histology. The result showed that the difference in change in inflammation at week 6 is significant between IL­-2C and PBS treated HUPO mice. In addition, HUPO mice treated with IL­-2C had higher %Treg in CD4+ cells. This was promising because it highlighted the possible role of Treg in the proliferation of RA. In the future, this experiment can be replicated with longer treatment time to determine whether the observed effect will diminish.

title: Inequality in America and The Incarceration System: Race, Crime and Criminal Justice
abstract: My research paper focuses on inequality in America specifically covering the incarceration system and the intersection of race and the criminal justice system. This is an important topic to study due to the high number of racially diverse individuals that are disproportionally affected and incarcerated due to the inequalities in the crime and criminal justice system. To investigate the extent of the issue, ethnographic interviews were conducted in a diverse sample of people by asking a set of questions on experience related to race, crime and criminal justice. The qualitative information gathered from the interviews and from an online class database was in line with the literature on the subject, in that there is currently a widespread problem of inequality in America with regards to race in the crime and criminal justice system. Recommendations were made in light of the findings and one of which was the importance of policy adjustments in the incarceration system. Further research is required to look into why policy adjustments are not being made to successfully serve all members of the society.

title: Influence of Socioeconomic Status and Sleep Quality on Risks for Obesity
abstract: Obesity is a multifactorial disease reflecting the interplay of biological and social factors.  Lower socioeconomic status (SES), food insecurity, and poor sleep quality are risks factors for obesity; yet, our understanding of the physiological mechanisms behind overweightness is limited.  Leptin, a hormone which modulates hunger, could be a potential mechanism because resistance can develop and lead to energy imbalances. Leptin levels tend to be elevated by low quality sleep; although evidence shows lower SES people sleep poorly, there is a gap in the literature quantifying the relationship between leptin and SES.  Hence, the objective of this research is to examine the influence of both sleep quality and SES on plasma leptin levels in a population undergoing rapid social change – the Yakut of northeastern Siberia.  Survey (household assets, sleep quality) and biometric (anthropometry and plasma samples) data from 210 Yakut adults were used to test  three hypotheses: (1) lower SES people experience lower quality sleep, 2) lower quality sleep correlates with higher leptin levels and 3) lower SES  is correlated with higher leptin levels. We used principle component analysis to build a wealth scale and sleep quality score and ran a regression for each hypothesis, controlling for sleep duration, fatness, sex and age. Although we found no correlation between sleep quality and leptin levels or SES and leptin levels, lower SES people experienced significantly lower quality sleep relative to their higher SES peers (p<0.05). Our results indicate that SES could play a significant role in impacting sleep, an important physiological process. Future research should explore how lower quality sleep influences health outcomes, particularly mental health and levels of other hormones like insulin.

title: Intersectionality and Social Identity: An exploration of meaning making and gendered racial identity among Black adolescent girls
abstract: There are few studies on social identity in psychological research that incorporate the multidimensionality and intersectionality of identity. More specifically, inquiries about how Black women experience identity have only more recently been explored (Jones & Day, 2018). The purpose of this present study was to examine the significance and meaning that Black adolescent girls attribute to their racial and gender identities, illuminating new themes and taxonomies that might exist for different demographics of Black women. Quantitative surveys and semi-structured interview data from 54 adolescent Black girls, attending an all-girls, mostly Black high school, were used in this study. Employing a mixed-method analytic procedure, we conducted a cluster analysis to identify emergent subgroups based on racial and gender centrality scores, which generated four social identity clusters. We then analyzed interview data using a grounded theory approach to further understand how the participants made meaning of their racial and gender identities, which generated a three-code scheme. Finally, we examined how the identity-clusters and qualitative meaning codes related to each other and measures of psychological well-being. Findings are discussed with implications and future research.

title: Investigating Chemical Synergy Strategy to Treat Neurodegenerative Diseases
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and other neurodegenerative diseases limit the human healthspan, during which life is spent in good health. These protein conformational diseases arise when specific aggregation-prone proteins misfold, leading to neuronal death. The cell maintains protein quality and prevents misfolding via stress responses like the heat shock response (HSR), which induces chaperone proteins to manage misfolding and protein aggregation. To reverse or abate protein misfolding in neurodegenerative diseases, we screened 30,000 compounds from the Chicago Biomedical Consortium library using human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells expressing a sensor which luminesces following HSR activation. We identified a group of epigenetic regulators, bromodomain and extra terminal domain (BET) and histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor compounds, that individually tripled luminescence. As BET and HDAC inhibitors may regulate HSR activity through different mechanisms, we test the hypothesis that combining these inhibitors can synergistically activate the HSR and improve protein folding. Our data found combining one BET and one HDAC inhibitor activates the HSR up to four times more than the sum of HSR activations by individual inhibitors; further study revealed that this synergistic interaction only exists for inhibition of specific HDAC proteins but exists broadly for various BET proteins. The BET and HDAC1 inhibitor combinations which most significantly increased HSR activation were used to treat rat neuronal Huntington’s disease model cells expressing a fluorescent aggregation-prone protein. Certain combinations led to a 50% reduction in protein aggregation, suggesting that these combinations could be used at a low dose in future therapeutics to treat neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Investigating soluble split-TEV to create new tools for synthetic protein circuits
abstract: Cell-based therapies are arising as promising technologies for a range of applications from cancer immunotherapy to regenerative medicine. Integral to cell-based therapies are synthetic gene circuits, which allow for programmable cellular response to external and internal signals. The ability to engineer and control protein-based signaling in cells is important for developing therapies that can respond quickly to the desired cues. Some recently developed protein-based circuits utilize split proteases, specifically, the tobacco etch virus protease (TEVp). TEVp has been split into two halves that reconstitute and maintain protease activity. To add new tools to the split-protein toolbox the function of different splits of TEVp were investigated. Soluble split-TEVp constructs with different positions of splits were developed. Upon addition of a small molecule, the split protease reconstitutes and releases a signaling molecule, through protease cleavage, that activates YFP reporter expression. The constructs were expressed in HEK 293FT cells and their expression was confirmed using a Western blot. To functionally test the panel of split-TEVp, the constructs were transfected into HEK 293FT cells, treated with the small molecule, and analyzed for YFP reporter expression through fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry. I compared these results with membrane bound split-TEVp results from the Leonard Lab and determined what trends persist and what new insights can be gained with how split-TEVp functions in the soluble environment. Researching soluble split-TEVp allows for a full investigation of the split-TEVp system and will add much needed insight and tools useful in protein-based circuits and cell-based therapy applications.

title: Joint Engagement of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder During Two Parent-Implemented Interventions
abstract: Establishing effective early intervention strategies for children with autism spectrum disorder is  the focus of a growing body of research. Teaching parents to implement language interventions  is an effective way to maximize the amount of intervention a child receives. Parent-mediated interventions have been shown to not only improve language skills, but also to build  foundational communication skills such as joint engagement (JE). In the present study, the  effects of directive and responsive intervention strategies on a child’s JE during a parent-mediated intervention were assessed using a behavioral coding system. The results of this study  indicate that children who were placed in the directive condition spent significantly more time in  higher forms of JE than children who were placed in the responsive condition. This suggests that  directive strategies could be more effective than responsive strategies when targeting a child’s JE.

title: Life Stress and Facial Expressions of Emotion in Individuals at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis
abstract: Psychosis is a devastating mental illness that is characterized by alterations in emotional functioning. A growing body of work has found links between life stress (e.g., abuse, bullying) and alterations in facial expressions of emotion (e.g., joy) among individuals with psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia. However, to date, there is limited work determining whether life stress is related to alterations in facial expressions of emotion prior to the onset of psychosis, among individuals described as clinical high-risk (CHR). This area of research is needed because potential relationships may inform our understanding of the etiology of psychosis given that many of these individuals are suggested to develop psychosis within a short window of time. As such, the current study sought to determine whether life stress was related to alterations in joy facial expressions of emotion among 75 CHR individuals and 79 age-matched healthy controls. We focused on joy expressions which were deduced from 1-minute video-recorded clinical interviews and measured on a second-by-second basis using the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) coding system. Measures of life stress included traumatic stress (e.g., experienced a life-threatening situation) extracted from the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV and interpersonal stress (e.g., bullying) assessed using a parent-report measure. Findings revealed that, overall, CHR individuals showed reduced joy expressions when compared to controls. Additionally, among CHR youth (but not healthy controls) a history of life stress was associated with lower joy facial expressions. These data shed light on our understanding of emotional alterations and psychopathology.

title: Looking into the subsurface: A geophysical investigation of a unique set of “spotted” hypersaline lakes in British Columbia, Canada
abstract: The search for evidence of extraterrestrial life on Mars requires understanding the preservation of  biosignatures in ancient environments. Several NASA funded projects are now being aimed at understanding terrestrial hypersaline environments and their role in preserving evidence of life, as these environments are analogous to past environments on Mars. A similar set of sulfate-dominated hypersaline lakes exist near Clinton, British Columbia, which have an unusual “spotted” appearance consisting of circular features with diameters ranging from ~1-10 m. However, the formation mechanism of the “spots”, or brine pools, and the thickness, depth, and lateral distribution of the subsurface salt layers of these lakes remain unknown. By traversing across the frozen lakes using a GSSI Profiler EMP-400 at transects spaced 1 to 10 m apart, I completed a frequency domain electromagnetic induction survey to map their subsurface salt concentrations. The results show that the salt distribution is indeed related to the spot formation of these lakes, yet varies between each. In several of the conductivity maps, we see low conductivity spots surrounded by high conductivity ridges, whereas the opposite is seen in others. The generated maps indicate areas of high conductivity inflow and high resistivity outflow. Ongoing data analysis is being completed to generate layered models of the subsurface conductivity which will allow for further interpretation. These results will be integrated into a larger body of work identifying how the distribution of salt relates to the unique geomorphology, geochemistry, and microbiology of the lakes, serving as critical information for ongoing astrobiological investigations.

title: Mathematical Modeling of U.S. Elections
abstract: Forecasting the outcomes of U.S. elections is a relevant and complex task that has been approached in many ways, most commonly incorporating statistics or proprietary methods that include some degree of subjectivity. Our approach differs from this convention in that we use multidisciplinary methods from applied mathematics. Specifically, we use a system of differential equations commonly employed for the study of disease transmission, to model the spread of political affiliation (Democrat or Republican) across states. We apply these models through programs written in R for data analysis and MATLAB for simulations. We are able to run thousands of simulations, with the addition of noise to account for uncertainty, to make a range of forecasts for election outcomes at the state level, specifically focused on swing states. The model’s forecasts for past presidential, senatorial, and gubernatorial elections after 2012 have accuracy comparable to popular forecasting sites. In this project, we are working to test the accuracy of the model with the 2004 and 2008 presidential elections. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of data-driven forecasting from a mathematical modeling perspective and suggests additional research in this field.

title: Parents’ Attachment in Conversation with their  Children: Impacts on their emotions and the relationship
abstract: Insecure attachment has well­documented implications for emotional functioning in romantic relationships, yet little research has explored how attachment (of the parent) may impact parent­ child relationships. The present laboratory­based study examined whether parents’ (N = 26; Mage = 48) attachment insecurity was related to emotions they and their children (Mage = 17) experienced during conversations. Parents’ insecure attachment (a composite of avoidant and anxious attachment; alpha = .85) was measured using the Adult Attachment Questionnaire. Parents and children engaged in (1) a neutral conversation about events of the day, (2) a conflict conversation about a topic of disagreement, and (3) a positive conversation about a topic of mutual enjoyment and reported on their emotional experiences after each conversation. In terms of parent’s attachment predicting their own experience, results showed that higher levels of parents’ insecure attachment were associated with higher levels of negative emotional experiences during the conflict conversation (r = 0.48, p= 0.015). This finding generalized across both anxious and avoidant attachment; was driven by negative emotions (e.g., anger); and was specific to the conflict conversation. In terms of parent’s attachment predicting their child’s experience, higher levels of avoidant attachment (and not overall insecure or anxious attachment) were associated with lower levels of positive emotions reported by their child (i.e., amusement, r = ­0.46, p = 0.022; excitement, r= ­0.43, p = 0.031). These findings highlight the downstream effects that parents’ attachment insecurity has on their own emotional functioning when navigating disagreements with their children and their children’s positive experiences.

title: Physiological and Affective Responses to Acute Aerobic Exercise, Mindfulness Training, and Combined Exercise and Mindfulness Training
abstract: Moderate-to-vigorous intensity physical activity (MVPA) has numerous health benefits. Yet, most adults are insufficiently active. Emerging data indicate incorporating mindfulness training may increase MVPA adoption and adherence. However, few studies have examined guided mindfulness practices during MVPA. This study examined the effects of an acute bout of MVPA, mindfulness training, and combined MVPA and mindfulness training on physiological and affective parameters. Using a within-subjects design, healthy adults (N= 30) completed three 36-minute-long counterbalanced conditions: a) mindfulness training only (MIND); b) MVPA only (MVPA), and c) MVPA+mindfulness training (PAMIND). MVPA conditions included a 10-minute warm-up, 6-minute cool-down, and a 20-minute brisk walk. Heart rate (HR), Blood Pressure (BP), Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE), and Feeling Scale (FS) were measured at rest, throughout the condition, and during recovery. The data was analyzed using within-subjects repeated measures ANOVA. Average, minimum and peak HR and RPE and average and peak systolic BP (SBP) were significantly higher while average, peak and minimum FS were significantly lower during both MVPA and PAMIND, independently, compared to MIND (p<0.001 for all). Average recovery HR was higher in both MVPA conditions, independently, compared to the MIND condition. Average and minimum RPE were significantly lower during PAMIND compared to MVPA (p<0.001, p=0.025). There were no other differences between the two MVPA conditions for peak, minimum or recovery values. The physiological response to MVPA alone and combined MVPA and mindfulness training were similar. However, lower reported perceived exertion could have implications for increased MVPA adoption and maintenance. Future work should explore these relationships further.

title: Point-of-Care Plasma Separator for HIV-1 Viral Load Testing
abstract: With the largest HIV epidemic in the world, South Africa has 7.7 million people living with HIV. Thus, it is crucial that patients have easy access to efficient viral-load testing. The current laboratory practice in South Africa takes several weeks or months for patients to receive their tests; in fact, 50% of patients never receive their results. The client Dr. David Kelso has therefore requested a method of separating plasma that will enhance an existing point-of-care (POC) system. A device will collect whole blood from a finger prick and ultimately isolate 70 μL of plasma. Furthermore, it must be compatible with a single-sample centrifuge to separate blood into its components: plasma, white blood cells, and red blood cells. The isolated plasma will later be combined with a buffer solution in order to fulfill the 1 mL plasma requirement of the existing technology, the Cepheid GeneXpert. The cartridge containing the plasma and buffer will be used in the GeneXpert to test for HIV-1 Viral Load. The team designed a blood collection device that relies on centrifugation and fluid balance to expel around 130 uL of blood into a capsule while retaining around 70 µL of plasma. A centrifuge that holds a singular collection device was designed as well. In addition to performing quantitative testing, two team members traveled to South Africa to perform user testing and observations in South African POC clinics. These members' insight was then incorporated in design iterations of both the centrifuge and collection device in order to best tailor the design towards the users’ needs.

title: Political transformations and their effects on foods in Peru, Venezuela and Argentina
abstract:
Eating is an indispensable part of the life of any animal, it takes up a great part of our time. However, for thousands of years, humans have been doing it differently, being food one of the clearest examples of how we have converted nature into culture. Eating is still a biological necessity that defines us merely as living beings, but the way we eat and cook can say a lot about how we organize our societies and how we relate with one another and our environments. Some have come as far as to say that what makes us different from animals are precisely our gastronomies.
This is why we believe that, by getting to know how foods and everything that surrounds them change, we can better understand ourselves and what matters to us. We think that, by understanding how politics can affect something as close to our daily lives as food, we can get a new perspective on the multiple effects that political changes have on people.
In this research which examines the ways in which political transformations have an impact on the gastronomies of Argentina, Venezuela and Peru, we analyzed during three months academic papers as well as articles from local magazines and newspapers that talked indirectly about foods. We then identified some of the topics that we saw repeatedly and developed an interview seeking to understand how these different topics related to each other and gave a meaning to foods. Finally, we compared and contrasted the results from our interview with other ideas that we had previously seen in our analyses.
As a conclusion, we found out that food in these countries plays a very important role in the development of a collective identity at multiple levels: familiar, local and national. Because of the social nature of food in these societies, it is especially vulnerable to political phenomena and two of the greatest ones so far have been migration and globalization. Both of them have had multiple consequences on foods like their loss of relevance within the family unit.

title: Quyud: Educational Constraints in Palestine
abstract: The right to education is a universal human right. It is fundamental for the existence of other human rights since it promotes independence and empowerment (Article 26, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN 1948; Article 13, International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, UN 1966). The research learns from Palestinians themselves how their educational journeys have been affected by the political, economic and social situation in the occupied West Bank. To study educational constraints in Palestine, I, along with my research partner Mariam Al-Dhubhani, collected ethnographic interviews from cities/villages in Areas A and B. Our field research in the West Bank encompassed 29 days over the summer of 2019, where we have conducted 58 interviews with students, teachers and workers about their educational journey in Palestine. The study looks at the constraints interviewees have faced as they pursue their basic human right, the right to education.

title: Regret and Psychosocial Adaptation
abstract: Previous research indicates that regret is a painful experience for people but often leads to enhanced self meaning and personal growth. In this study, we employ a narrative approach to explore the architecture and coping methods of regret experiences in late midlife adults. We relate variation in regret narratives told by 163 adults aged 55 to 57 to psychosocial adaptation, conceptualized in terms of psychological well-being and Erikson’s adult-developmental factors of generativity and ego-integrity. Two coders analyzed interview transcripts of regret narratives for numerous content categories, including type of regret, source of regret, degree of resolution (coming to terms with, making peace with, solving the problem of) the regret, and hopefulness for the future. The qualitative results illustrate the diversity and richness of regret experiences in late midlife and flesh out the expression of 12 different coping methods for dealing with negative life experiences. The quantitative results provide empirical support for the hypothesis that degree of regret resolution is positively associated with overall psychosocial adaptation. Findings are discussed in terms of the role of the bidirectional relationship between regret resolution and psychosocial adaptation, as well as the role of regret experiences more generally in life stories and in late midlife development.

title: Sea level rise threatens the Florida Keys
abstract: A chain of low-lying islands, the Florida Keys, are already affected by sea level rise. The website States at Risk says Florida has over 1.5 million people threatened by inland flooding and 3.5 million people threatened by coastal flooding. The report “Climate-Sensitive Hazards in Florida” says that Florida’s Monroe County, which is comprised of the Keys, is one of three counties in the state with the highest level of risk from just over 11 inches of sea level rise. I conducted interviews with Florida Keys environmental experts, government figures and residents to put together three podcast episodes about what sea level rise looks like in the Keys, how it affects the Keys’ economy, and what residents think about it. Plant and animal species, such as South Florida Slash Pines and Key Deer, are losing their habitats as oceans rise and saltwater encroaches on their territory. Keys residents are also impacted by sea level rise, which causes nuisance flooding and worse storm surges and threatens future permanent inundation of some areas of the islands. The Florida Keys are making changes as sea levels rise, and every change comes with an immense cost. These podcasts contribute to a very necessary dialogue on addressing and adapting to climate change, and the audio format allows for the immersion of audiences in the issue as the sounds of the Keys and voices of its residents fill their ears.

title: Seeing What You Want: Prior Belief Biases Perception of Correlation in Scatterplots
abstract: We think data is definitive, but our perception of it contains bias from expectations and motivations. For example, when Democrats and Republicans view the same depiction of global temperature trends, Democrats see an increasing trend, while Republicans see overall flatness. Could prior beliefs bias our perception of relations depicted in visualized data? We empirically examine how prior beliefs influence correlation estimations in scatterplots. We recruited 295 adults from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk and trained them to extract correlations from scatterplots. Participants viewed four no-context scatterplots (axes ‘X’ and ‘Y’) and the same four scatterplots, but with context (axes with real-world variable pairs). Participants also rated their agreement with statements describing the variables’ relationship, which were used to measure prior beliefs about the pairs. People who more strongly believed a relationship depicted with the real-world variables estimated the correlation to be stronger in the plot with context than in the plot without context. People who did not believe in the relationship estimated the correlation to be weaker for the context plots than for the no-context plots. These results suggest that real-world context around a scatterplot can generally bias correlation estimation, and for belief-triggering topics, the amount of bias can depend on the strength of the belief.

title: Sexual Self-Insight
abstract:
Attachment style deeply affects people’s experiences in their relationships, including their
experiences with sex. For example, anxiously attached people are more likely to have sex with their partners due to insecurity, rather than to experience sexual pleasure (Schachner & Shaver, 2004). Thus, anxiously attached people may lack insight into what they actually enjoy sexually. We propose the novel construct of Sexual Self-Insight and hypothesized that anxiously attached people may have low Sexual Self-Insight. We collected a sample (N=265) of MTurk participants, all whom were in currently in a relationship. The participants were surveyed on Sexual SelfInsight [a measure adapted from the existing Self-Concept Clarity scale (Campbell et al. 1996)], attachment style, and commitment to their relationship. As hypothesized, anxiously attached individuals experienced less Sexual Self-Insight as indicated by the moderate, negative correlation between anxious attachment and Sexual Self-Insight (r = -.604; p < 0.001). Sexual Self-Insight was positively associated with relationship commitment, as was hypothesized. Moreover, lower Sexual Self-Insight mediated the association between anxiety and lower commitment (indirect effect = -.17; 95% CI = -.25, -.09). Therefore, it is possible that our research findings– that anxious attachment is associated with less Sexual Self-Insight-- is a product of the phenomena found by Schachner and Shaver. Results from this study further elucidate challenges that anxiously attached individuals face in romantic relationships.

title: Simulating the period-recovery yield of Eclipsing Binaries in Star Clusters with LSST
abstract: We present a study of the period-recovery capability of the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST​) for eclipsing binary stars in star clusters. Unlike binaries in the galactic field, dynamical encounters within the dense environment of a star cluster can modify the orbital parameters of binaries stars, by changing the periods and eccentricities and exchanging in different companions. Therefore, eclipsing binaries in star clusters may allow for insights into both the intrinsic properties of the binary’s component stars, as well as the dynamical histories of the binary population. For our simulations, we use COSMIC to generate and evolve populations of binaries specifically catered to each of the thousands of galactic open and globular clusters (e.g., matching the cluster ages, metallicities, periods at the hard-soft boundary, etc.). We generate light curves, in the LSST filters and expected cadence and accounting for the expected photometric precision of LSST, for each observable eclipsing binary, using the ellc code. We then attempt to recover the orbital period for each observed binary through a Lomb-Scargle periodogram, using gutsy software. We compare the baseline cadence proposed for LSST to a colossus cadence that samples the galactic plane (where most open clusters reside) more evenly. In this poster, we present expected recovery statistics for eclipsing binary stars in the galactic open and globular star clusters for both of these proposed observing strategies.

title: Single exposure to inaccurate statements leads to reliance on false information
abstract: There is increasing concern about the spread of false content online. It has therefore become urgent to determine how and the extent to which individuals are influenced by misinformation. Past research has found that reading single sentences of false information—even just a single time—can increase its perceived truthfulness. This project attempts to extend prior work by characterizing whether people will reproduce false information after a single exposure. Participants were presented with 81 single sentence statements, which were either accurate (e.g., “dried grapes are called raisins”), inaccurate (e.g., “dried grapes are called prunes”), or a semantically-related neutral statement (e.g., deer meat is called venison”). Half of the general knowledge statements were easy/well-known and half were hard/unknown. After a brief distractor task, participants were presented with 81 free response questions related to the previously-presented sentences (e.g., “what are dried grapes called?”). We measured how often participants answered with the incorrect lure (e.g., “prunes”) after reading each of the three sentence types. Participants produced the incorrect lure significantly more often after reading inaccurate as compared to accurate or neutral statements. This was most robust for statements that were unknown rather than known by participants. These findings suggest that people will rely on inaccurate information provided to them one time as a single sentence, even if they should know better. However, it is especially likely when the information is less-familiar, indicating that people are most likely to reproduce false information when they have less prior knowledge on the topic.

title: Spatial Patterns of Shipping-induced Ground-level Ozone and Particulate Matter over the Great Lakes Region
abstract: Shipping over the Great Lakes (GL) and its tributaries influence regional air quality through emissions of primary pollutants that form ground-level ozone (O3) and particulate matter (PM2.5). O3 is a secondary pollutant, as it is not directly emitted and forms when primary pollutants react. Although some PM2.5 constituents are directly emitted, many are secondary pollutants. With over 100 GL-commercial ports, these pollutants can have deleterious health effects. Despite this, there has been little quantification of shipping emissions in inland water bodies, including the GL. The purpose of this study is three-fold: assess the spatial distributions of O3 and PM2.5, the total air quality impact of shipping, and the significance of precursors, including nitrogen oxide, sulfur dioxide, and volatile organic compounds. Shipping emissions data is provided by the National Emissions Inventory. We use the Weather Research and Forecasting-Community Multi-scale Air Quality model to simulate the baseline current-state and no-shipping-emissions (NSE) cases. Shipping-induced O3 raised the 24-hour average ambient (24AA) O3 concentration by 0.06 parts per billion-volume (ppbV). However, the 8-hour average ambient (8AA) O3 concentration is 0.03 ppbV less in the baseline case. Both cases exhibit greater O3 levels over GL water bodies and decreased levels over some urban areas. Shipping-induced PM2.5 raised the 24AA PM2.5 concentration by 0.03 ug/m3 and the 8AA by 0.01 ug/m3. These results, especially the regional differences and non-linear distribution of O3 and PM2.5 on areas of greater versus lesser degrees of urbanization, warrant continued study of the transport of shipping-induced pollutants and their precursors.

title: Stories of Activism
abstract:
How are activists formed? What prompts individuals to break the barrier of apathy and take 
action to fight for social change? Through field observation and one­on­one interviews with 
young climate activists in Chicago, this project attempts to answer these questions by exploring the motivations behind youth activism. Building on foundations created by existing micromobilization research, this project zooms in on individual stories and decisions, attempting to understand how young people today transition from simply caring about a cause to taking concerted action. Interviews with young activists and sympathizers were completed and analyzed through qualitative coding, and demonstrated three recurring catalysts for climate activism: education, media, and experiences with nature. The interviews also found several barriers: fear and helplessness, and the absence of personal stake or pathways to action. These findings have implications for initiatives to increase youth involvement in climate activism, suggesting that providing young people with opportunities to engage with the outdoors and educating them on the realities of human­induced environmental degradation may lead to greater participation. They also present broader implications for discussions on micro­mobilization and recruitment for activist organizations, suggesting that youth political apathy can be combated by early, targeted, multimedia and experiential education paired with clearly articulated pathways to action. Although there may not be a formula for the creation of politically engaged citizens, three ingredients ­ knowledge of the problem, a clear personal stake, and the presentation of solutions or action steps ­ may significantly increase involvement in social movements.

title: Surveying Current Generation in Metal Nanolayers: The Impact of Rust
abstract: Global energy consumption is projected to grow by nearly 50% by 2050. To meet this demand, researchers are exploring new materials which induce electricity by moving ionic fluids over electrically conductive or semi-conductive layered surfaces, such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, and dielectric-semiconductor structures. Some report an energy conversion of up to 30%. The Geiger group has discovered a similar system by flowing saltwater over thin nanolayers of earth-abundant metals, like iron, which are prepared in a single step over large areas. This phenomenon could be implemented under flowing water at water treatment plants, as well as in estuaries, fjords and even living bodies, to passively generate power and monitor the environment. However, the mechanism of current generation in this system has not been fully defined. Further development of mechanistic understanding is necessary to predict and control this potentially useful energy converter. To explore hypothetical mechanisms, assorted metal nanolayers were fabricated from transition metals using electron-beam physical vapor deposition. Each nanolayer’s capacity for current generation was quantified and compared to properties of the metal and its naturally occurring oxide. This survey suggests electron transfer between multiple oxidation states in the metal oxide greatly enhances current generation. With this knowledge, future work will explore how electrostatic interactions at the interface between the aqueous phase and metal oxide surfaces generate charge carriers, and to a greater extent when multiple oxides are accessible.

title: Swimming Upstream: Decreasing Salmon Populations in the Columbia River Basin  through Infrastructure and its Impacts on Indigenous Welfare
abstract: Since 1854, when tribal treaties began to allocate sustainable quantities of fish to different actors along the Columbia River, there has been tension between governing state bodies and those populations reliant on fish for sustenance and livelihood. This project critically analyzes the systemic impedance of the Yakama tribe settled along the Columbia River to salmon and their gradual and ongoing subjugation in the context of environmental conflict. Additionally, I use (GIS) mapping to demonstrate water culverts’ effect on drastically decreasing salmon spawning, resulting in turn in significant stress on the fish, a staple resource for the Yakama. This paper connects urbanization and infrastructure in Washington state with an environmental crisis that disproportionately impacts native groups in the area. This research will bring to light how governing bodies do not prioritize indigenous welfare, especially in the context of environmental justice.

title: Tea with Mama
abstract:
Tea Time with Mama is a documentary about Afnan and her mother as they recollect their
memories of their homeland in Yemen before they moved to Qatar. They also talk about the
sacrifices and role of a mother while they spend tea time together. The motivation and rationale for this project are to illustrate the concept of home is not where you are but rather who are with. As Afnan and her mother recollect their memories in Yemen, they found comfort with each other while they make tea together.  Afnan Tag is also a proud wildcat in Northwestern University in Qatar and we found it heartwarming when she told us the story of her family. It only made us realized how everyone has a story to tell.

title: Team Performance in Long-Duration Space Exploration
abstract: Long-duration space explorations (LDSE) planned by NASA to the moon in 2024, and Mars in 2030, will face extended communication delays between the crew and mission control, as they travel farther from Earth. Thus, it is critical to construct crews that can operate autonomously of mission control. Previous research suggests that social network relationships among team members impact their performance on job-related tasks. To extend this work to LDSE, we gathered data from 12 crews who completed 30-45 day missions, operated by NASA, to mimic work in LDSE. Crew members were surveyed on their interpersonal relationships and evaluated on their performance on tasks representing four domains from McGrath’s (1984) Group Task Circumplex: developing new ideas (Generate), negotiating solutions or compromises (Negotiate), choosing among alternatives (Choose), and executing tasks that require skills (Execute).  Our analyses indicate that the structure of positive affect, conflict, and leadership relations between crew members impact their performance on these tasks. Specifically, crews that have a member who provides (centralized) leadership to all other members perform worse on tasks that require crews to develop new ideas (Generate) but better on tasks that require them to solve survival scenarios (Choose), compared to crews without centralized leadership. We also observe that crews with a greater amount of conflict reported among members performed better on Choose and Execute tasks than crews that reported lower conflict. The methodology and empirical findings reported in this study contribute to optimal crew selection efforts for forthcoming LDSE missions to the Moon and beyond.

title: The Escherichia coli thiB Thiamine Pyrophosphate Riboswitch Uses Strand Invasion as a Primary Mechanism of Gene Regulation
abstract: Riboswitches are RNA elements that regulate gene expression by changing their structure upon binding small molecule ligands in their environment. Development of synthetic riboswitches for use as molecular biosensors is an active area of research which requires that riboswitch gene regulation mechanisms are more clearly understood. Some mechanisms, such as those elucidated for the  Escherichia coli lysC  riboswitch, are dual­acting to prevent translation initiation and trigger mRNA decay. Others, like those of the  N. crassa  NMT1 riboswitch, use alternative splicing to regulate the development of mature mRNA. This project focuses on the E. coli thiB TPP  riboswitch, which represses gene expression when exposed to thiamine  pyrophosphate (TPP). We investigate the hypothesis that this riboswitch functions through an RNA strand invasion mechanism. This was tested through site­directed mutagenesis of functionally critical parts of the riboswitch, such as the ligand binding aptamer region and the invading strand sequence. In­vivo gene expression assays were utilized to determine the minimal structures necessary for the riboswitch to conduct efficient regulation. It was found that in absence of TPP, the strand invasion mechanism occurs. Here, the invading strand base pairs with nucleotides in the aptamer region, which prevents sequestering of the ribosome binding site (RBS) to allow gene expression. In high concentrations of TPP, the thiB riboswitch adopts a stable conformation which blocks strand invasion, thereby preventing gene expression. Upon further research of their common regulatory pathways, these conclusions will be useful for the development of synthetic riboswitches for molecular biosensing applications in the future.

title: The I in Community: Social Trust for First-Year Students
abstract:
Reena Burt 

Faculty Advisor: Mesmin Destin

The I in Community: Social Trust for First-Year Students

Social trust plays a central role in our lives. According to the current literature, social trust is related to social and economic outcomes ranging from happiness and tolerance to civic engagement and societal economic growth to democratic functioning and decreased crime levels. Despite its importance, social trust has been declining in the U.S. since the 1980s. A trend driven by younger generations. Surprisingly, there is limited research on what impacts young adults’ social trust levels and why it is declining. To better understand the decline of social trust in younger generations, my study examines how specific identities, values, and character traits relate to young adults’ social trust. I conducted a mixed-methods study with 96 online survey responses and 9 semi-structured interviews from first-year students at a private mid-western university. Results showed that values of vertical collectivism (i.e. high family integrity and sociability with in-groups) are positively associated with trust in home communities whereas values of vertical individualism (i.e. competition and hedonism) are positively associated with trust in the university community. Identifying with more agent social identity groups was positively associated with social trust in the university community. These findings highlight two potential predictors of social trust that are understudied– individual and collective values and identity. This research has implications for institutions that seek to create a more trusting environment for all on college campuses.

title: The Lucky One
abstract: The topic of sexual assault and harassment has been an issue I've always been passionate about fighting against. Specifically, I wanted to write about child abuse because there have been cases around the world in numerous cultures where child abuse is not taken seriously because pedophilia is a taboo topic and numerous families will care more about reputation and/or family bonds than protecting children from abusers. The method I took to this was creative writing because if described accurately, even if vaguely, the imagination that someone could do that to a child can still be haunting. I made the main character older so readers can understand the effects that abuse have on children, even after being saved. In addition, I wanted to show the consequences of pedophilia not being stopped by family members because the abuser will just continue to harm other children. Hopefully, the conclusion readers will take from the short story is that these topics need to be addressed and learned about it or the cycle will never end. The Lucky One adds to the conversation that children might forget their abuse due to memories being blocked due to trauma, which adults need to be aware about in order to take the issue more seriously.

title: The Role of the Atrophin Domain in the Function of AFF1-SEC as a Transcription Inhibitor
abstract:
Abstract
The identity of a cell is determined by which genes are expressed and in what quantities they are expressed. In skin, progenitor cells self-renew and differentiate to form epidermal tissue; this process requires strict dynamic regulation of transcription elongation by releasing RNA Polymerase II from its paused state and is therefore known as a transcription activator. The SEC contains two mutually exclusive scaffolding subunits, AFF1 and AFF4. Therefore, the SEC can exist in two variants, but it is unknown but how much these variants differ in function. Dysregulation of the SEC has been identified in leukemia, but the role of the SEC during healthy tissue differentiation is unknown. Here we show that in addition to functioning as a transcription activator, the SEC is capable of inhibiting the transcription of differentiation markers by using AFF1 as its scaffolding protein. We hypothesize that the Atrophin domain located on the AFF1 protein is necessary for AFF1-SEC to function as an inhibitor. To test this, we first overexpressed AFF1 in keratinocytes. Over-expression of AFF1 downregulated transcription of differentiation genes, implying that the SEC utilizes AFF1 to suppress expression of differentiation genes in order to maintain cells in the progenitor state. Then, we overexpressed a variant of the AFF1 protein with the Atrophin domain deleted. This had no observable effect on the transcription of differentiation genes, suggesting that the domain is necessary for AFF1-SEC to function as a transcription inhibitor.

title: Variations between American States Maternal Mortality Data and Its Consequences on National Metrics
abstract: Since 2007, the United States has not produced an official maternal mortality statistic. As health work uses metrics as one of its main tools for policies and practices, the lack of an official number is a point of concern for those that work on maternal child health. To understand the potential difficulties in producing a national metric, this research project focused on how states data collection can hinder the creation of official numbers. This meant that the date methods like terminology used, following of CDC and/or WHO guidelines, frequency that maternal death records are collected, that each state used was collected and compared. The research found that producing one national metric would be very difficult due to the different methods including timelines and definitions that each state follows for their individual data production. Consequently, even if the US produced data, the metric would have many limitations and not be an accurate or precise number that would be most beneficial for policy making. While the lack of an official maternal mortality metric from the US for over the past 10 years may seem like a mistake and lack of political interest in the field, it can also be seen as saving resources by not producing official numbers that would be an inadequate representation of maternal health in the US. Furthermore, this project showcases that producing a valuable maternal mortality metric depends on more than the work of federal agencies as the lack of organization and inconsistency between states prevents the National Center for Health Statistics from having useable information for the metric.

title: Visual Attention in Children
abstract: Speech perception is inherently multimodal during face-to-face conversations: we both hear and see the talker. Infants are able to integrate audiovisual speech cues from early in life. Recent evidence suggests that they also flexibly shift their visual attention to a talker’s lips in conditions when speech is unfamiliar. The present study aimed to extend this work. Specifically, we tested the hypothesis that children will flexibly alter their visual attention to talkers when speech input is degraded. The rationale for this study is that naturalistic environments of children often contain background noise that disrupts the fidelity of the acoustic parts of speech. Participants were typically-developing children between 3 and 5 years of age. To quantify visual attention, we utilized an eye-tracking paradigm which assesses the location and duration of a participant’s eye gaze to the talker and images of known words as speech was unfolding, in quiet and in the presence of two-talker background speech presented at 10 dB signal-to-noise ratio. Consistent with our hypothesis, results showed that children visually fixated the talker to a greater extent in the background speech condition than in the quiet condition. The presentation will include discussion about how children’s speech recognition accuracy with or without visual speech cues as well as preliminary data from children with hearing loss. The data informs us about how young children flexibly alter their visual attention to talkers in less than ideal listening environments.

title: What Identities Warrant the Lens of Intersectionality in Psychology and Human Development Research?: A Comprehensive Literature Review
abstract: Coined by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989, intersectionality is a paradigm for understanding how individuals’ multiple identities converge. Although intersectionality has long been used by sociologists and ethnic studies scholars, it has only recently been taken up by psychologists as an analytic tool for understanding identity. This project is a substudy of an ongoing systematic literature review intending to identify and analyze how intersectionality is defined and measured in psychological research on identity processes. In particular, we aim to identify which identities psychologists are examining through the lens of intersectionality. We collected texts (n=1361) from PsycInfo, a leading database of psychological scholarship. Next, we conducted inclusion coding to select US-based empirical research focusing on identity processes, resulting in a final yield of 359 peer-reviewed articles (n=167), dissertations (n=179), and book chapters (n=11). Using NVivo 12, we content coded all remaining texts for sample demographics, methodologies used, and identities studied. Our discovery-based process resulted in a much more diverse list of identity categories than expected based on the foundational race/class/gender focus of intersectionality. Although many texts focus on racial-ethnic (n=307), gender (n=297), sexual (n=135), and class (n=91) identities, the presence of other categories (i.e., work, religious, and immigrant identities) in at least 30 texts each was a particularly interesting finding. The breadth of identities studied indicates that intersectionality is being applied in a range of ways, highlighting the need to examine how intersectionality is being operationalized across disciplines.

title: Who am I Now? Identity Formation and Self-Perception Following Parental Death in Adolescence
abstract: Over 1.5 million adolescents experience the loss of a parent, adding an additional layer of stress to a developmental period characterized by extensive transitional processes. Despite the prevalence and impact the loss of a parent has on adolescent development, there is surprisingly little research that examines how parental loss shapes development as youth transition out of adolescence and into emerging adulthood. The present study sheds light on the adolescent grieving process during the transition into emerging adulthood. Results show that many adolescents do not receive the adequate support needed for a healthy grieving process, causing adolescents to bottle up their emotions and grief. The grieving process shapes adolescents, especially as they enter emerging adulthood, building empathetic character and a deeper understanding of their role in their surrounding environment. Overall, my research sheds light on how such loss impacts one’s identity and understanding of the self during adolescence, in addition to uncovering what can be done to support adjustment and encourage healthy development following the loss of a parent.

title: “It Wasn’t Made for Him”: Examining Female-Led Superhero Films Wonder Woman and Captain Marvel and the Internet Commentary that Followed.
abstract:
Recently, there has been a public push for the film industry to improve female representation; subsequently, DC and Marvel released female­-lead films Wonder Woman and Captain Marvel to critical praise and record box office figures. Strictly looking at industry measures of success (critics’ reviews and box office totals) it would appear that the film industry and movie­going public are demanding more films with similar female representation. However, public opinion cannot be captured by critical interpretation and viewership alone; it is important to understand how audiences feel after viewing a film and which aspects did or did not resonate with them. With my research, I studied a portion of the discourse spread about these films on the internet to uncover an untold aspect of their public reception. I read and coded meaningful sentiments from the first 250 IMDb user reviews for each film to evaluate audiences’ perspectives on themes. This sentiment speaks to changes within the gender culture of the film industry as well as the viability of future female­-lead films. In general, I found that user critics on IMDb were much less
welcoming to these films as previous measures of success would indicate and would often
express their discontent about similar factors including the film’s representations of feminism, the   actress’   behavior   both   on   and   off­screen,   and   how   the   films   compared   to   previous installments in their respective cinematic universes. I combine these findings with influence from theories about spectatorship, feminism, the superhero genre, paratexts, and convergence culture.
